Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, for a commutative unital ring $R$. Cap with its relative fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $p$,
$$S_p:H^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M,A;R),\qquad T_p:H^p(M,A;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R).$$
Here both maps send a class $a$ to $a\cap[M,A]$ in the displayed target. Empty boundary recovers Poincaré duality. Disconnected and empty manifolds are included. AC is inherited only from the exhaustion and local universal-coefficient arguments in Poincaré duality.

Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, where $R$ is a commutative unital ring and the orientation is supplied on $M\setminus A$. Its **relative fundamental class** is the unique class
$$[M,A]\in H_n(M,A;R)$$
whose restriction at every interior point is the prescribed local generator. Existence and uniqueness, including manifolds with closed components, are proved in [[lem-a-collar-identifies-boundary-local-homology-with-the-pair-fundamental-class]].

The **induced boundary orientation** is the orientation whose local generator at $x\in A$ is the restriction of $\partial[M,A]$, where $\partial$ is the homology pair connector. The same lemma proves that these restrictions are generators and form a continuous section. Thus
$$\partial[M,A]=[A]$$
for this orientation. In tangent-then-inward coordinates its generator is $(-1)^n$ times the tangent generator for the product orientation: this is the outward-normal-first convention. Each component inherits its sign from the supplied interior orientation; there is no further independent selection of signs.

If $A$ is empty, this is the absolute fundamental class and the boundary class is zero. In dimension zero the boundary is empty. Empty $M$ and the zero coefficient ring give the unique zero class. These definitions and their well-definedness use no AC.

For composable chain maps in an abelian category
$$C_\bullet\xrightarrow{f}D_\bullet\xrightarrow{g}E_\bullet,$$
there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(D,C;f)\to H_n(E,C;gf)\to H_n(E,D;g)\to H_{n-1}(D,C;f)\to\cdots.$$

If $Z\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, then
inclusion $(X-Z,A-Z)\to(X,A)$ induces isomorphisms
$H_n(X-Z,A-Z;G)\cong H_n(X,A;G)$ for every $n$.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth 3-manifold as in [[def-oriented-smooth-cobordism]], with closed, possibly disconnected boundary $\Sigma$, and let $i:\Sigma\hookrightarrow M$ be inclusion. Extend the direct-sum intersection form of [[def-intersection-form-on-the-homology-of-a-closed-oriented-surface]] to $H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb R)$. The boundary kernel

$$\lambda_M=\ker(i_*:H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb R)\to H_1(M;\mathbb R))$$

is Lagrangian. If $\Sigma$ is empty, this means $\lambda_M=0$ in the zero symplectic space.

Use the Wall-form Maslov convention of [[lem-maslov-index-four-lagrangian-cocycle]]. Let $B\subseteq\overline V\oplus W$ be a finite-dimensional real Lagrangian relation, where the product symplectic form is $-\omega_V\oplus\omega_W$. Write $B(L)=\{w:\exists v\in L,(v,w)\in B\}$ and $B^t(Q)=\{v:\exists w\in Q,(v,w)\in B\}$. For Lagrangians $L,P\subseteq V$ and $Q,R\subseteq W$,

$$\mu_V(L,P,B^t(Q))+\mu_W(B(L),Q,R)=\mu_W(B(P),Q,R)+\mu_V(L,P,B^t(R)).$$

Consequently, for composable Lagrangian relations $A:V_0\to V_1$, $B:V_1\to V_2$, $C:V_2\to V_3$ and specified Lagrangians $\lambda_i\subseteq V_i$, the integer correction $m(B,A)=\mu_{V_1}(A(\lambda_0),\lambda_1,B^t(\lambda_2))$ satisfies

$$m(B,A)+m(C,BA)=m(C,B)+m(CB,A).$$

It vanishes for either identity relation, is additive on direct sums, and for graphs of symplectic isomorphisms $f_1,f_2$ equals $\mu(f_2f_1\lambda_0,f_2\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$. No injectivity, transversality or equal-dimension hypothesis on a general relation is imposed.

Let $(V,\omega)$ be a finite-dimensional real symplectic vector space and let $L_1,L_2,L_3$ be Lagrangian subspaces. Put

$$U_{123}=\frac{L_1\cap(L_2+L_3)}{(L_1\cap L_2)+(L_1\cap L_3)}.$$

For $a\in L_1\cap(L_2+L_3)$ write $a+b+c=0$ with $b\in L_2,c\in L_3$. The form

$$\psi_{123}([a],[a'])=\omega(a,b')$$

is well-defined, symmetric, and nondegenerate. Define $\mu(L_1,L_2,L_3)=\operatorname{sign}(\psi_{123})$. For any four Lagrangians,

$$\mu(L_1,L_2,L_3)+\mu(L_1,L_3,L_4)=\mu(L_1,L_2,L_4)+\mu(L_2,L_3,L_4).$$

Use the category, $D,d_i,\kappa$ and dualities of [[lem-colored-fr-surgery-and-coupon-cancellation]]. For a connected standard genus-$g$ marked surface $t$, put

$$X_{t,i}=W_1^{\epsilon_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes W_n^{\epsilon_n}\otimes\bigotimes_{r=1}^g(i_r\otimes i_r^*),\qquad V_t=\bigoplus_{i\in I^g}\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf1,X_{t,i}),\qquad d(i)=\prod_r d_{i_r}.$$

For disjoint surfaces take tensor products and set $V_\varnothing=\mathbb C$. Opposite raw coupon coordinates are $\bigoplus_i\operatorname{Hom}(X_{t,i},\mathbf1)$, with composition pairing. With the standard spine handlebody caps and their reflected opposite caps, the normalized capped-cylinder Gram pairing is

$$Q_t(y_j,x_i)=\delta_{ij}D^{g-1}d(i)^{-1}y_ix_i.$$

Its inverse correction is $N_t|_i=D^{1-g}d(i)1$, extended multiplicatively across surface components. For a fixed special surgery graph $\Omega$ representing a connected parametrized graph bordism $M$, let $m$ and $B$ be its surgery-component count and linking matrix. Define $A_M$ by the raw testing-coupon functional $y(A_Mx)=D^{-m-1}\kappa^{-\sigma(B)}F(\Omega;y,x)$, with finite surgery-color sum understood, and set $Z_\alpha(M)=N_{\Sigma_{\rm out}}A_M$. Then

$$Z_\alpha(M)^j_i=\kappa^{-\sigma(B)}D^{-m-1+\chi(\Sigma_{\rm out})/2}d(j)F_0(\Omega;i,j).$$

Here $\alpha$ denotes the actual reference cap meridians and $F_0$ includes the exact tensor-Hom projections defined below. These fixed-presentation operators satisfy the cylinder, ball, empty and disjoint-union laws. For stacked presentations of composable bordisms,

$$Z_\alpha(M_2M_1)=\kappa^{\sigma(B_1)+\sigma(B_2)-\sigma(B_{\rm comp})}Z_\alpha(M_2)Z_\alpha(M_1).$$

The signatures here are the actual matrices, including the indicated added annuli. No Maslov identification is assumed in this lemma. For disconnected $M$, use the product over its connected components, equivalently the exponent $-m-b_0(M)+\chi(\Sigma_{\rm out})/2$. Independence under a complete relative presentation calculus is a separate theorem; this result proves the exact normalization and algebra of its local cap/stacking models. No unweighted anomaly-free functor is asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For any symmetric finite-dimensional real form $q$ on $E$ and subspace $V$, one has $\operatorname{sign}(E)=\operatorname{sign}(q|_V)+\operatorname{sign}(q|_{V^\perp})$, allowing all restrictions to be degenerate. Split off a nondegenerate complement to the radical of $q|_V$, reducing to an isotropic $V$, and discard the ambient radical without changing signatures. For an isotropic basis $v_i$, choose dual vectors $u_j$ with $q(v_i,u_j)=\delta_{ij}$ and replace $u_i$ by $u_i-\frac12\sum_jq(u_i,u_j)v_j$. The resulting pair span has matrix $\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&I\\I&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ and signature0. Its orthogonal complement is the nondegenerate reduction of $V^\perp/V$, so its signature is that of $V^\perp$. If $V$ met the discarded ambient radical, first discard those basis vectors. Reintroducing the first nondegenerate orthogonal summand proves the asserted formula.

A surgery trace $W_L$ is $B^4$ with framed two-handles. A handle core capped by a Seifert surface has self-intersection equal to its framing; distinct capped cores intersect by the oriented linking number, counted by pushing their Seifert surfaces normally. Thus its intersection matrix is the actual linking matrix $B_L$, and $\sigma(W_L)=\sigma(B_L)$ even when singular. To identify the stacked trace cut, let the separating sphere bound a three-ball $P\subset B^4$ and take its collar $P\times I_t$. The old $L_1,L_2$ handles lie on their respective side hemispheres. Each new joined-handle surgery circle crosses the equator twice; parametrize its new handle as $h_r=D^2\times D^2\cong I_s\times I_t\times D_z^2$. Only its two opposite attaching patches $\{s=\pm1\}\times I_t\times D_z^2$ meet the middle collar, along two disjoint $D^2\times I_t$ disk products. Its other attaching patches $I_s\times\{t=-1\}\times D_z^2$ and $I_s\times\{t=+1\}\times D_z^2$ lie in the two side hemispheres. The zero framing is exactly the matching of these $z$ coordinates without a rotation; it is available from the explicit paired disk-product presentation in [F4]. Round only the small product corners. This specifies which portions of each original attaching region lie in each piece.

Put $E=H_2(W)$ with its absolute intersection form and $V=\operatorname{im}[H_2(W_1)\oplus H_2(W_2)\to H_2(W)]$. Interior cycles in different pieces are disjoint, and the restriction within each is its original intersection form. Thus the pullback of the form on $V$ is the direct sum of the forms of $W_1,W_2$. Its inclusion kernel is radical because its image intersects every cycle trivially; quotienting by it changes no signature. Hence $\operatorname{sign}(q_W|_V)=\sigma(W_1)+\sigma(W_2)$, and step 1.1 reduces the entire defect to the form on $V^\perp$.

Let $C$ be the union of $P\times I_t$ and those new handles with only their $s=\pm1$ patches attached to that collar. Relative to $C$, each handle is $I_s\times(I_t\times D_z^2)=D^1\times D^3$, attached along $S^0\times D^3$. It is therefore a four-dimensional one-handle relative to the middle collar, although it was a two-handle relative to the original whole attaching circle. All disjoint disk products match, giving the literal product $C=[P\cup(\bigsqcup_r I_s\times D_z^2)]\times I_t=U_G\times I_t$. In particular $H_1(C)=\mathbb R^G$, $H_2(C)=0$, $\sigma(C)=0$. The two side intersections are exactly $(P\times\{\pm1\})\cup(\bigsqcup_r I_s\times\{\pm1\}\times D_z^2)\cong U_G$. The complementary side pieces are the original four-ball halves with their old $L_i$ handles: rounding the product indentations changes only boundary collars; no whole new handle remains on either side. Thus the actual decomposition is $W_{L_{\rm comp}}=W_{L_1}\cup_{U_G}(U_G\times I)\cup_{U_G}W_{L_2}$ with these exact faces. This avoids the false ordinary-handle claim: $B^4$ with $G$ whole attaching-circle two-handles instead has $H_2$ of rank$G$ and is not this middle product.

Use smooth singular chains subordinate to product collars, or a finite smooth subdivision respecting all faces. Excision gives $H_2(W,M_0)=H_2(W_1,M_0)\oplus H_2(W_2,M_0)$. For $z\in H_2(W)$ let $z_i$ be its relative image. Its intersection with any $y\in H_2(W_i)$ is the evaluation of the image of $z_i$ in $H_2(W_i,\partial W_i)$ on $y$: all transverse intersections are in the interior of $W_i$, so enlarging the allowed relative boundary from $M_0$ to $\partial W_i$ does not alter them. Perfection in [F1] therefore gives $z\in V^\perp$ exactly when both those relative images vanish. The triple sequence and excision contain $H_2(M_i,\Sigma)\to H_2(W_i,M_0)\to H_2(W_i,\partial W_i)$. Hence for such a $z$ choose $s_i\in H_2(M_i,\Sigma)$ mapping to $z_i$, and write $a_i=\partial s_i\in K_i$. The boundary of $z$ in the sequence of $(W,M_0)$ is zero, so $a_1+a_2$ maps to zero in $H_1(M_0)$. Thus $a_0=-a_1-a_2\in K_0$ also bounds a relative chain in $M_0$.

Conversely take a triple $(a_1,a_0,a_2)\in K_1\oplus K_0\oplus K_2$ with sum0. Choose actual smooth singular one-cycle representatives for $a_1,a_2$, define $a_0=-a_1-a_2$ at the chain level, and choose bounding two-chains $S_i\subset M_i$. Their boundaries may be made those exact one-cycles by adding their homology corrections in face collars. Thus their sum is a closed two-cycle with product collars and no unaccounted central two-chain in $\Sigma$. Push its faces slightly into $W$, obtaining $z(a)\in V^\perp$ by step 3.1. Different bounding choices in $M_1,M_2$ change it by boundary classes and hence globally radical classes; choices in $M_0$ change it by classes in $V\cap V^\perp$, radical on $V^\perp$. For an arbitrary original $z$ of step 3.1, the constructed $z(a)$ has the same image in $H_2(W,M_0)$, so $z-z(a)$ is in $\operatorname{im}H_2(M_0)\subset V$ and in $V^\perp$, again radical. The triple construction therefore surjects onto the nondegenerate reduction of $V^\perp$.

Near $\Sigma$ choose $u\ge0$, $v\in\mathbb R$ and $p\in\Sigma$, with $\operatorname{or}(W)=du\wedge dv\wedge\operatorname{or}(\Sigma)$, $W_1=\{v\le0\}$, $W_2=\{v\ge0\}$, $M_0=\{v=0\}$, $M_1=\{u=0,v\le0\}$ and $M_2=\{u=0,v\ge0\}$. The $M_0$ face of $W_1$ has orientation $-du\wedge\operatorname{or}\Sigma$; its outward boundary vector at $u=0$ is $-\partial_u$ and gives precisely $\operatorname{or}\Sigma$. The outer face of $W_1$ is $-dv\wedge\operatorname{or}\Sigma$, so the convention $\partial W_1=M_0-M_1$ gives $\operatorname{or}(M_1)=dv\wedge\operatorname{or}\Sigma$ and its boundary has that same $\Sigma$ orientation. Similarly $\operatorname{or}(M_2)=-dv\wedge\operatorname{or}\Sigma$ and its boundary agrees. These coordinates realize exactly the Statement's signs. A bounding strip along a normal ray coordinate $t$ pointing away from the corner has orientation $-dt\wedge a_i$, giving boundary $a_i$ at $t=0$.

All outside-corner intersections can be removed explicitly. The three faces have disjoint tubular neighborhoods away from a fixed corner collar. For the first and second surfaces supported on the same face choose two distinct constant small normal levels into $W$: distinct positive $u$ levels for $M_1,M_2$, and distinct $v$ levels for the seam $M_0$. Even if their underlying chains in a three-face meet along curves, their normal levels separate them. Different faces remain in disjoint neighborhoods. In the annular transition to the corner normal fan, interpolate the two same-face levels to two ordered endpoints on the boundary of that face's angular sector. Linear interpolation preserves their order; the three sectors are disjoint there. Hence no intersections occur in the transition annulus either. For both triple chains use the exact chain equality $a_1+a_0+a_2=0$ of step 4.1, so no extra central $\Sigma$ surface is hidden in this construction. The perturbations are realized on the finitely many smooth chain pieces with product collars; bilinear intersection counts add over these pieces, so the argument applies even when a representing singular chain has multiple components or self-intersections.

Move the second triple's junction in the normal half-plane to $(\epsilon,\epsilon)$, leaving its negative-$v$ ray directed from that point toward the negative-$v$ boundary ray, its positive-$v$ ray toward the positive boundary ray, and its seam ray toward increasing $u$. Choose the already ordered transition paths of step 6.1. In the central disk the only crossing is then between the first seam ray and the second negative-$v$ ray. The first tangent is $+\partial_u$ and the second points toward decreasing $v$, so their determinant in the ordered normal plane $(\partial_u,\partial_v)$ is negative. The two oriented surface tangent bases are $(-t_0,a_0,-t_1',a_1')$. Moving the first surface's $\Sigma$ tangent past the second surface's normal tangent gives one minus; the two displayed prefixed minus signs cancel. Thus the four-dimensional sign is minus the normal crossing sign times the $\Sigma$ crossing sign, yielding $q_W(z(a),z(a'))=\omega(a_0,a_1')=-\omega(a_1,a_0')$. The last equality is symmetry of the Walker form for order $(K_1,K_0,K_2)$, using isotropy and the sum-zero equations. step 6.1 excluded every other intersection. Therefore the pullback remaining form is $-\psi_W$. The surjection of step 4.1 carries radicals to radicals, and its kernel is radical because the target pairing pulls back to this form. Its nondegenerate reduction is consequently isometric to that of $V^\perp$. Combining this with step 1.1, step 2.1 proves $\sigma(W)=\sigma(W_1)+\sigma(W_2)-\mu_W(K_1,K_0,K_2)$. Disconnected faces give orthogonal sums throughout.

Absorb $U_G\times I$ into the first trace by a boundary collar extension, preserving its other cap faces and signature. Apply step 7.1 to its remaining gluing face with the second trace. For $r>1$ middle components, first cut $P$ along the $r-1$ disjoint separating disk products of [F4]'s family-meridian model. They separate precisely the specified arc families; their thickened compressions split the middle product into the disjoint products $U_{g_q}\times I_q$, with all other side pieces unchanged. The redundant final family-meridian in the alternative all-$r$ graph is a separated zero-framed trace handle with matrix$[0]$ and signature0; omit it for the actual cut. Thus the same argument applies componentwise, and the incidence-component connected-sum reduction in [F4] adds only zero-signature trace blocks.

The corner surface orientation in step 5.1 is opposite the canonical middle object orientation: it is induced from the incoming face of $M_2$, and $\partial M_2$ contains the negative of that object. The corner kernels identified with its canonical $H_1$ are $K_1=R_1(\alpha_0)$, $K_0=\alpha_1$, $K_2=R_2^t(\alpha_2)$. Indeed Mayer–Vietoris after capping the incoming boundary of $M_1$ says that a middle class dies exactly when it is homologous in $M_1$ to an element of the cap kernel $\alpha_0$; this is precisely $R_1\alpha_0$. The identical outgoing-cap argument gives $K_2$, and the common actual handlebody has kernel $\alpha_1$ by its definition. These use the individual bordisms, not inclusion maps into their final composite. Negating the surface orientation negates the entire Walker form. step 7.1 with the actual trace cut of step 1.2, step 2.2, step 8.1 therefore gives $\Delta\sigma=+\mu_W(R_1\alpha_0,\alpha_1,R_2^t\alpha_2)=\mu_\alpha$. Substituting into [F4] gives $Z_\alpha(M_2M_1)=\kappa^{-\mu_\alpha}Z_\alpha(M_2)Z_\alpha(M_1)$.

This sign can also be checked directly against Turaev's printed convention: his form on $a=a_1+a_2\in L_3$ is $h(a,b)=\omega(a_2,b)=\omega(a_2,a_1')=-\omega(a_1',a_2)=-\psi_W(a',a)$. Symmetry gives $\mu_T=-\mu_W$. His surgery parameter is $\Delta=p_-$, so $D/\Delta=\kappa$ and his anomaly $\kappa^{\mu_T}$ is exactly $\kappa^{-\mu_W}$. This is a sign comparison only; the local Wall proof above does not cite that source theorem as its proof. In particular preserving the prescribed composition $n_{\rm comp}=n_1+n_2+\mu_W$ requires weight action $\kappa^{+n}$, since $\kappa^{-n}$ would duplicate instead of cancel the computed anomaly.

No arbitrary real $\lambda$ needs realization by a geometric handlebody. Keep the actual reference cap meridians $\alpha$ and set $w(R)=\mu_W(\lambda_0,\alpha_0,R^t\alpha_1)+\mu_W(R\lambda_0,\alpha_1,\lambda_1)$, $a(R)=-w(R)$. These spaces are Lagrangian by [F3], even for noninjective relations. To compute its coboundary use [F3]'s proved associative category of weighted relations. The diagonal weight-zero relation $J:(H,\lambda)\to(H,\alpha)$ has the weight-zero diagonal inverse: their composition corrections are $\mu(\lambda,\alpha,\lambda)=0$. For a relation $R$ between the reference objects with weight0, the arrow $J_{\rm out}^{-1}\circ R\circ J_{\rm in}$ between the $\lambda$ objects has exactly weight $w(R)$, by the two displayed middle-space corrections. For composable $A,B$, cancelling adjacent $J$ arrows calculates its weight as $\mu_\alpha+w(BA)$; composing the two $\lambda$ arrows calculates it as $w(B)+w(A)+\mu_\lambda$. Associativity equates these actual weights. Therefore $a(BA)-a(B)-a(A)=\mu_\alpha-\mu_\lambda$, without defining an integer by the desired equality.

Define $Z(M,n;\lambda)=\kappa^{n+a(R_M)}Z_\alpha(M)$. The exponent in its composite is $n_2+n_1+\mu_\lambda+a(BA)-\mu_\alpha=n_2+a(B)+n_1+a(A)$ by step 10.2, so step 9.1 proves strict weighted composition. The correction vanishes when $\lambda=\alpha$, and for the identity relation it is $-\mu(\lambda,\alpha,\alpha)-\mu(\lambda,\alpha,\lambda)=0$. The cylinder and tensor/empty laws of [F4] therefore persist; direct sums add both Maslov terms and $a$. A weight increase by1 acts by $\kappa$ with no anomaly-free assumption. Equivalently the connected block formula is $\kappa^{n+a(R_M)-\sigma(B)}D^{-m-1+\chi(\Sigma_{\rm out})/2}d(j)F_0(\Omega;i,j)$, with [F4]'s multiplicative disconnected version. This proves all stated signature, cap-reference and weight assertions while leaving genuine relative presentation/move completeness to its own theorem. Full AC is inherited precisely through [F1], and countable choice through [F4]; the new form reductions and bases are finite.

citations.quote: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). For every compact collared triad $(W;M_0,M_1)$ there are an adapted excellent Morse function $f:W\to[0,1]$ and an adapted complete downward gradient-like field $X$, both agreeing with the product model on smaller neighborhoods in the fixed collars: $f=t_0/3$ near $M_0$, $f=1-t_1/3$ near $M_1$, and $X$ is its negative Riemannian gradient for a metric that is a product metric there. Here **adapted complete** has the collar-extension meaning of [[def-morse-function-adapted-to-a-cobordism]]: $X$ is the restriction of a complete smooth field on a boundaryless collar extension of $W$; a trajectory is followed in $W$ only until it exits a face.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(W;M_0,M_1)$ be a compact triad with adapted
excellent Morse function $f$ and adapted field $X$. Then there are an adapted
complete downward gradient-like field $X'$ and an adapted Morse function $g$
with the same critical points and indices as $f$, equal to $f$ near
$\partial W$, such that all critical points of a given index $k$ lie at one
common level and the common levels increase strictly with $k$: there is a
strictly increasing $\phi:\{0,\dots,n\}\to(0,1)$ with
$g(p)=\phi(\operatorname{ind}p)$ for every critical point $p$. After composing
with a boundary-fixing increasing diffeomorphism of $[0,1]$ one may take
$g(p)=(\operatorname{ind}p+1)/(n+2)$. Consequently the handle decomposition
attaches all index-$k$ handles at the single level of index $k$, before all
handles of index $k+1$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(W;M_0,M_1)$ be a compact triad and let $f$ be
an adapted Morse function whose critical points of index $k$ all lie at one
level $c\in(0,1)$, with no critical point of another index at $c$ and no other
critical value in a neighbourhood of $c$. Then the
sublevel just above $c$ is obtained from the sublevel just below $c$ by
attaching disjoint $k$-handles, one for each index-$k$ critical point.
Equivalently, handles of equal index attached at one level may be regarded as
attached simultaneously or successively in any order, the result being the same
up to diffeomorphism fixing the incoming face and respecting the lower sublevel up to homotopy of pairs. On the common attached-stage model, reordering disjoint attachments fixes its entire lower stage. Handles of equal index may
be reordered freely, and attaching embeddings may be changed by isotopy of the
attaching region.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open and let $Y:U\to\mathbb R^2$ be a $C^1$ vector
field with flow $\Phi$. Let $\mathcal O^+(y)=\{\Phi_t(y):t\ge0\}$ be a positive
orbit whose closure $K_0=\overline{\mathcal O^+(y)}$ is compact and satisfies
$K_0\Subset U$. Put $K=\omega^+(y)=\bigcap_{T\ge0}
\overline{\{\Phi_t(y):t\ge T\}}$, and assume $K$ contains only finitely many
equilibria (zeros of $Y$). Then exactly one of the following forms holds:

(i) $K$ is a singleton equilibrium;

(ii) $K$ is one regular periodic orbit;

(iii) $K$ is a nonempty finite set $E$ of equilibria together with at least one
regular trajectory, and every regular point of $K$ lies on such a trajectory
whose alpha- and omega-limit sets are points of $E$.

The family of connecting trajectories in (iii) need not be finite. The
conclusion uses no choice principle beyond the ambient Euclidean completeness.

Let $\gamma$ be a simple closed piecewise $C^2$ regular plane curve that
bounds a supplied positively oriented disk region $D$, has finitely many
ordinary corners, and has matching unit tangents at the identified endpoint.
Write $k_{\mathrm{plane}}$ for the signed curvature of its unit-speed
parametrization with respect to the positive quarter-turn $J$ of the standard
orientation, and $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m$ for its signed exterior angles at the
corners. Then

$$\int_\gamma k_{\mathrm{plane}}\,ds+\sum_{j=1}^m\alpha_j=2\pi .$$

The identity is independent of the regular parametrization because
$k_{\mathrm{plane}}\,ds=d\theta$ for a continuous tangent-angle lift $\theta$ on
each smooth piece.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. For each $p\in M$, let
$\gamma_p:I_p\to M$ be the maximal integral curve through $p$, and set

$$ \mathcal D:=\{(t,p)\in\mathbb R\times M:t\in I_p\}, \qquad \Phi(t,p):=\gamma_p(t). $$

Then $\mathcal D$ is open in $\mathbb R\times M$, each fibre $\mathcal D_p$ is
an interval containing $0$, the map $\Phi:\mathcal D\to M$ is smooth, and
$\Phi$ is the unique maximal local flow generated by $X$.

Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a compact interval, and let $X_t$ be a smooth
time-dependent vector field on $M$ such that

$$ \bigcup_{t\in J}\operatorname{supp}(X_t) $$

is contained in a compact subset $K\subseteq M$. Then there is a global evolution
operator $\Psi_{t,s}:M\to M$ for all $s,t\in J$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold without
boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold, and let
$F\colon M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy such that $F_t:=F(\cdot,t)$ is an
embedding for every $t\in I$. Suppose $F$ is constant near the ends of $I$:
there is $\varepsilon\in(0,\tfrac12)$ with $F(x,t)=F(x,0)$ for $t\le\varepsilon$
and $F(x,t)=F(x,1)$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon$ and all $x\in M$. Then for every
open neighbourhood $W$ of the image $F(M\times I)$ there is an ambient isotopy
$H\colon N\times I\to N$ such that

$$H_t\circ F_0=F_t\quad\text{for every }t\in I,$$

$H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, each $H_t$ is a diffeomorphism of $N$, and $H_t$ is the
identity outside $W$ for every $t$. Moreover $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\in[0,\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}]$ and
$H_t=H_1$ for $t\in[1-\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},1]$.
Under countable choice, every smooth manifold, also with boundary, admits a Riemannian metric.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

For fixed attaching and product-collar data, two compatible smooth monotone roundings of a handle attachment are diffeomorphic by an isotopy supported in that collar. The diffeomorphism is the identity outside the collar.

Fix $n\ge0$. By the cobordism equivalence relation
([[thm-smooth-cobordism-is-an-equivalence-relation]]) the closed smooth
$n$-manifolds are partitioned into cobordism classes
([[def-unoriented-smooth-cobordism-of-closed-manifolds]]). Let
$$\Omega_n^{O}:=\{\,[M]\;:\;M\ \text{a closed smooth }n\text{-manifold}\,\}$$
be the set of these classes in the bounded model convention below, and let
$$\Omega_n^{SO}:=\{\,[Q,o]\;:\;(Q,o)\ \text{a closed oriented smooth }n\text{-manifold}\,\}$$
be the set of oriented cobordism classes
([[def-oriented-smooth-cobordism]]).

**Set-size convention.** For each $n$ use the set of all closed smooth
$n$-manifold structures on subsets of $U_n=\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb N$,
and in the oriented theory include the orientation datum, before taking the
quotient by cobordism. Every closed smooth $n$-manifold has such a model:
compactness gives a finite chart cover $(V_j,\varphi_j)_{j<k}$, and the map
$x\mapsto(\varphi_j(x),j)$, with $j$ the least index for which $x\in V_j$,
is injective into $U_n$. Transport the topology, maximal atlas, and supplied
orientation along this injection; its image is diffeomorphic to the original
manifold. This uses only a finite chart cover, not a choice of a model for every
manifold simultaneously. Two transported models are diffeomorphic, and a
cylinder of [[lem-cylinders-give-reflexivity-of-cobordism]] with outgoing
collar composed with a diffeomorphism's inverse shows they are cobordant (orientation-preservingly in the oriented case). Thus $[M]$
means the unique class of any such model. Products and disjoint unions are
returned to this set of models in the same way; their class is independent of
the transport.

**The operation.** Disjoint union of manifolds defines operations
$$[M]+[N]:=[M\sqcup N]\quad\text{on }\Omega_n^{O},\qquad [Q,o]+[R,p]:=[Q\sqcup R,\,o\sqcup p]\quad\text{on }\Omega_n^{SO},$$
where $o\sqcup p$ is the orientation of the disjoint union whose restriction to
each summand is the given orientation, and finite disjoint unions carry the transported component atlases
([[prop-countable-disjoint-unions-of-fixed-dimensional-smooth-manifolds-are-smooth-manifolds]]);
for summands with boundary the same construction uses half-space charts.
Finite union preserves compactness and combines finitely many countable bases,
so this boundary extension requires no countable choice.
The class of the empty $n$-manifold is the displayed **zero** $0$: it is
null-cobordant and is a two-sided identity for the operation, since
$M\sqcup\varnothing$ is canonically diffeomorphic to $M$
([[def-null-cobordant-closed-manifold]]).

**Well-definedness.** The operations are independent of the chosen
representatives. If $W_i$ is a bordism from $M_i$ to $M_i'$ for $i=0,1$, then
the disjoint union $W_0\sqcup W_1$ carries the canonical smooth structure of a
compact $(n+1)$-manifold with boundary
$\partial(W_0\sqcup W_1)=(\partial W_0)\sqcup(\partial W_1)$, the collars
$\theta_0^0\sqcup\theta_0^1$ and $\theta_1^0\sqcup\theta_1^1$ are smooth
embeddings onto collar neighbourhoods of the boundary parts, and the
decomposition of the boundary into the two parts is again open and closed;
hence $W_0\sqcup W_1$ is a bordism from $M_0\sqcup M_1$ to
$M_0'\sqcup M_1'$. In the oriented case, orienting the disjoint union by the
given orientations makes the disjoint union of the oriented bordisms an
oriented bordism between the disjoint unions, because the induced boundary
orientation is computed componentwise and each summand carries its required
sign. Thus $[M_0\sqcup M_1]=[M_0'\sqcup M_1']$ whenever $[M_i]=[M_i']$, and
similarly in the oriented theory. The class of a finite disjoint union is
computed from the canonical smooth structure on disjoint unions; no further
choice is made.

**Deferred axioms and the forgetful map.** That these operations satisfy the
group axioms (associativity, commutativity, identity and inverses) is not
asserted here: it is proved in the following theorem, together with the
finiteness of the inverse in the unoriented theory. The **forgetful map**
$$\Omega_n^{SO}\longrightarrow\Omega_n^{O},\qquad [Q,o]\longmapsto[Q],$$
sends the oriented class of a closed oriented $n$-manifold to its underlying
unoriented cobordism class; it is well defined because an oriented bordism
between two oriented manifolds is in particular a bordism between their
underlying manifolds, so oriented cobordant manifolds are cobordant.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a Banach space, $a<b$, and let $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$ in the sense of [[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces]]. If there is $C\ge0$ with $\|\varphi'(s)\| \le C$ for all $s\in(a,b)$, then $\|\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)\| \le C(b-a)$. In particular, if $\varphi$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ and $\varphi'=0$ there, then $\varphi$ is constant.

derivations.claim: **Smooth disk isotopy: vector fields.** Put $Q=[0,1]^2$. Let $\mathcal F$ be its orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms equal to identity near the boundary. Enlarge this to $\mathcal E$ consisting of diffeomorphisms equal to identity near the left, top and bottom edges and of the form $(x,g(y))$ near the right edge. For $f\in\mathcal E$, the nonzero plane field $v=f_*e_1$ is $e_1=(1,0)$ near every edge. Lift $v:Q\to\mathbb C^\times$ through the exponential to a smooth logarithm $\ell$ with value zero at the lower left corner. Existence follows by continuation of local logarithms on the simply connected square; uniqueness makes them agree. The boundary collar is connected, so $\ell=0$ there. Set $v_t=\exp((1-t)\ell)$. These fields are nonzero, equal $e_1$ on a common collar, and interpolate from $f_*e_1$ to $e_1$.

**Surface cutting and twists.** All surfaces below are compact, connected and oriented; original boundary collars remain fixed. A twist on an annulus is $(\theta,u)\mapsto(\theta+2\pi b(u),u)$, where $b$ equals zero and one at opposite ends. The negative sign gives its inverse. A smooth disk-and-bands model follows from [F1] in dimension two: cancel a maximal tree of zero-handles and joining bands. Sliding band ends in boundary collars puts intersecting pairs into one-holed-torus blocks; remove such blocks successively. With no intersecting pair the remaining model is a disk with holes. These are smooth operations: each band slide moves adjacent attaching intervals along an embedded arc in a disk by the supported velocity flow [F3, F4]. In particular cutting a nonseparating curve lowers genus by one. For two disjoint nonseparating curves, the complement is connected or has two components each incident to both curves: a component incident only to one would make that curve separating. No conversion of an arbitrary topological homeomorphism into a diffeomorphism is used.

**No trapped trajectory.** Extend each $v_t$ by $e_1$ beyond the square. A forward trajectory entering the left edge cannot cross the horizontal boundary collars and can exit only through the right. If it never exits, its closure is compact in a slightly larger rectangle; there is no equilibrium. By [F2] its limit set is a periodic orbit. Uniqueness makes such an orbit a smooth simple closed curve, whose tangent winding is $\pm1$ by [F2]. But $\ell$ extends by zero, so its restriction to that orbit gives a single-valued tangent-angle lift and winding zero, a contradiction. The same argument backwards shows every interior trajectory reaches the left edge in finite negative time. Thus trajectories from the left parametrize the whole square without overlap.

**Intersection reduction.** For nonseparating smooth curves $\alpha,\beta$, remove innermost bigons until they are in transverse minimal position. Each removal is a smooth disk-supported isotopy lowering the finite intersection count by two. If $N=|\alpha\cap\beta|\ge2$, take an arc $\delta$ of $\beta$ between consecutive intersections. If its endpoints lie on opposite banks of $\alpha$, join $\delta$ to a subarc of $\alpha$, round corners and shift one endpoint across $\alpha$. The resulting simple curve $\gamma$ crosses $\alpha$ once and $\beta$ at most $N-1$ times: outside the small rectangle about $\delta$ it follows a parallel copy of that subarc. Its single crossing makes it nonseparating. If the endpoints lie on the same bank, band surgery gives two curves $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ disjoint from $\alpha$, with oriented classes $[\alpha]=[\gamma_1]+[\gamma_2]$. The class of $\alpha$ in the homology of the capped surface is nonzero; hence one $\gamma_i$ has nonzero capped class and is nonseparating. Each uses one complementary subarc of $\alpha$ and two parallels of $\delta$; pushing these off $\beta$ gives at most $N-2$ intersections with $\beta$. Induction on $N$, with bases zero and one, gives a path of nonseparating curves with successive intersections zero or one. All moves avoid protected collars.

**Smooth time normalization.** Let $\Gamma_t(s,y)$ be the flow from $(0,y)$ and $r_t(y)>0$ its first right-edge exit time. At exit $\partial_s\Gamma_t^1=1$, so the implicit function theorem and [F3] give smooth exit times. Compactness gives $0<m\le r_t(y)\le M$. Choose a smooth function $\rho\ge0$ zero on endpoint collars of total length $c<m$ and positive elsewhere. The function $a\mapsto\int_0^1\exp(a\rho(u))\,du$ is smooth strictly increasing with image $(c,\infty)$. Its smooth inverse defines $a(r)$ for $m\le r\le M$. Put $\chi(x,r)=\int_0^x\exp(a(r)\rho(u))\,du$. Then $\chi(0,r)=0$, $\chi(1,r)=r$, $\partial_x\chi>0$, $\partial_x\chi=1$ near the endpoints, and $\chi(x,1)=x$. Therefore $E_t(f)(x,y)=\Gamma_t(\chi(x,r_t(y)),y)$ is a smooth diffeomorphism in $\mathcal E$. Its inverse follows the trajectory to the left and inverts $\chi$. At $t=0$ it is $f$, and at $t=1$ it is identity.

**Replace disjointness by one crossing.** For disjoint nonisotopic nonseparating curves $a,b$, cut along both. In a connected complement join one bank of $a$ to one bank of $b$; cutting along this arc leaves the surface connected because it joins distinct boundary components. Join the other two banks by a second disjoint arc. If the complement has two components, join its $a$-bank to its $b$-bank in each component. Regluing and rounding gives a curve $d$ crossing each once; it is nonseparating since it crosses $a$ once. Thus every zero-intersection step can be replaced by two one-intersection steps. The intersection-one graph is connected for every positive genus, including genus one with arbitrary boundary.

**Fix the right edge.** For $h\in\mathcal E$, write $h(x,y)=(x,g_h(y))$ near the right edge. For an increasing interval diffeomorphism define $G_s(g)(y)=(1-s)g(y)+sy$, still increasing. Choose $\beta(x)=1$ near the left and zero near the right, and put $\Psi_h(x,y)=(x,G_{\beta(x)}(g_h^{-1})(y))$. This is identity near the left, top and bottom and equals $(x,g_h^{-1}(y))$ near the right. Thus $p(h)=\Psi_h\circ h$ lies in $\mathcal F$, with $p|_{\mathcal F}=\mathrm{id}$. For $f\in\mathcal F$, the family $p(E_t(f))$ is the required smooth isotopy relative to a common boundary collar. Rounding the square corners away from its support gives the disk assertion. A smooth time reparametrization makes this and subsequent isotopies stationary at their endpoints for concatenation.

**Transport by twists.** A neighborhood of two curves $a,b$ with one crossing is a one-holed torus. Cutting it to a square, the twists act on the coordinate arcs by the two elementary shears. The three shears $T_aT_bT_a$ exchange the two coordinate directions, reversing one. Their square acts as $-I$, so it reverses the orientation of $a$. These representatives are supported in the one-holed torus and fix its boundary collar. By step 3.2, a finite twist word takes any nonseparating curve to any other; the squared three-twist word corrects any unwanted reversal of its orientation.

**Planar induction and its kernel.** Every diffeomorphism of a disk with $n$ holes, fixed on boundary collars, is smoothly isotopic to a twist word. For $n=0$ use step 4.1. Cap one inner hole by a parametrized disk $D$. By induction subtract a twist word for the extended map, choosing its curves to miss $D$ by isotopy. The remaining extended map has a smooth isotopy to identity. Its restriction to $D$ is a loop of disk embeddings. The kernel is generated by moving the center of this disk along loops and rotating its frame; the disk-family and lifting constructions establish this assertion, including the compact-family and homotopy-lifting details.

**Genus reduction and the whole first jet.** For positive genus choose an oriented nonseparating curve $a$. Step 4.2 gives a twist word $h$ such that $hf$ preserves its class and orientation. An ambient isotopy makes the image curve exactly $a$. Correct its restriction to $a$ in an annular collar: the convex interpolation of an increasing circle lift with the identity is increasing. Now the resulting map $k$ fixes $a$ pointwise and, in collar coordinates $(\theta,u)$ with $a=\{u=0\}$, has derivative $A(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}1&a(\theta)\\0&b(\theta)\end{pmatrix}$ with $b>0$. Define $J_t=\begin{pmatrix}1&-ta/b\\0&1-t+t/b\end{pmatrix}$, so $J_0=I$ and $J_1=A^{-1}$. Write $J'_tJ_t^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&c_t\\0&d_t\end{pmatrix}$. The supported field $\rho(u)(c_t(\theta)u,d_t(\theta)u)$ has a flow $\psi_t$ fixing the curve and with derivative $J_t$ there, by the variational ODE. Consequently $K=k\circ\psi_1$ has its entire first jet equal to identity on the curve, including the tangential normal shear.

**Disk families reduce to frames.** For a smooth compact family of disk embeddings $e_z$, choose a metric by [F5] and put $p_z=e_z(0)$. The geodesic ODE [F3] and the inverse function theorem give exponential coordinate disks at all centers with one uniformly positive radius. For uniformly small $r>0$, put $E_z(w)=\exp_{p_z}^{-1}(e_z(w))$ near the source origin. The embeddings $\exp_{p_z}(E_z(rqw)/q)$ for $0<q\le1$ extend smoothly at $q=0$ to $\exp_{p_z}(r(de_z)_0w)$, because $E_z(rqw)/q=r\int_0^1(dE_z)_{srqw}w\,ds$. All images remain in the exponential disks; for positive $q$ they are compositions of restriction, coordinate diffeomorphism, dilation and inverse coordinate diffeomorphism, and at zero their linear derivatives are invertible. This formula is metric-defined and agrees on overlaps for interval and square parameter families. Thus shrinking the disks and then applying this deformation reduces families to their centers and positive linear frames. The positive scale and positive triangular part of such a frame are contractible, leaving a unit tangent direction. Shrinking changes the base disk along a path; its monodromy transport only conjugates endpoint maps, and conjugation takes twists to twists about transported curves.

**Two-parameter lifting without disk-group contractibility.** For a smooth family $e_{s,t}$, extend each disk embedding slightly beyond its source boundary locally in parameters. On its compact graph in the product of parameter space and surface prescribe $V_{s,t}(e_{s,t}(w))=\partial_s e_{s,t}(w)$. Local smooth extensions exist in product charts. A finite cover and a partition of unity patch them, since all values agree on the graph; a cutoff keeps support away from protected surface collars. Integrate in $s$, with $t$ stationary, using [F3]. This yields smooth ambient diffeomorphisms carrying $e_{0,t}$ to $e_{s,t}$. If the disk family is constant in $s$ on a protected parameter edge, extend it constantly on a parameter collar so the lifted velocity vanishes there. The same construction lifts paths in $t$. Thus for a based loop homotopy constant at $t=0,1$, the endpoint diffeomorphisms of its lifts vary by a smooth isotopy fixing the disk pointwise. Two lifts of one path differ by a family fixing the disk at every time; their endpoints give the same relative mapping class. This proves the required independence and homotopy invariance of monodromy, using no assertion about disk-group connectivity.

**Kernel generators are twists.** The planar surface retracts onto a finite graph, so center loops are words of simple loops. Its tangent bundle is trivial, and the remaining frame loop has integer rotation number. A center push along a simple loop is the product of two twists on its annular neighborhood: in coordinates $(\theta,u)\in S^1\times[0,2]$, add $2\pi tu$ for $u\le1$ and $2\pi t(2-u)$ for $u\ge1$, smoothing the two pieces while preserving the central circle. At $t=1$ the two halves give $T_{\mathrm{left}}T_{\mathrm{right}}^{-1}$. A full rotation of the disk frame is a twist about its boundary. The construction is away from other collars and descends to the disk complement. Steps 6.1–3.3 therefore express every kernel element as a twist word, completing the planar induction in step 5.1. Only surjectivity onto the kernel was needed, not injectivity of a Birman sequence.

**Remove the remaining collar germ.** Choose the unique small angular lift of $K-\mathrm{id}$ near the curve. Uniform Taylor estimates give $K-\mathrm{id}=O(u^2)$ and $dK-I=O(|u|)$. Let $\rho_\delta$ equal one for $|u|\le\delta$, zero for $|u|\ge2\delta$, with derivative bounded by $C/\delta$. The maps $L_s=\mathrm{id}+s\rho_\delta(K-\mathrm{id})$ have derivative $I+O(\delta)$, including the cutoff derivative term. For small $\delta$ lift the collar to $\mathbb R^2$ and extend the displacement by zero in the normal direction. The derivative of this periodic displacement has norm less than $1/2$. Applying [F7] to the displacement on each straight line segment gives its Lipschitz constant at most $1/2$. Thus the lift is injective by the estimate $|L_s(x)-L_s(y)|\ge|x-y|/2$, and is surjective: for each target $z$, iteration of $x\mapsto z-(L_s(x)-x)$ has successive differences decreasing by a factor at most $1/2$, hence is Cauchy in $\mathbb R^2$ and converges to the required preimage. Its local inverses are smooth. Equivariance under the angular period descends this diffeomorphism to the annulus, and extension by identity gives a diffeomorphism of the surface. Since $L_1=K$ on a smaller collar, $L_1^{-1}K$ is identity there. Cutting along that collar lowers genus by one and adds two fixed boundary collars. Induction on genus, based on step 8.1, proves generation by twist words. In closed genus zero first fix a disk using the disk-motion construction and its frame adjustment; the complement is the disk case of step 4.1. Thus the sphere case is also smooth, without the topological Alexander trick.

**Heegaard splitting.** Suppose $X$ is connected. Apply [F1] with empty faces and choose a regular level between indices one and two. Its lower sublevel $H$ consists of zero-handles and one-handles. It is connected: two- and three-handles have connected attaching regions and cannot join components, whereas $X$ is connected. Contract a spanning tree of the finite zero/one-handle graph. Each tree edge joins two balls through a tube; straighten its attaching disks in ball collars, identifying the union with a ball. Iteration gives a ball with $g$ one-handles, the standard handlebody $H_g$. Reading the upper sublevel upside down gives another connected handlebody. Their common boundary has Euler characteristic $2-2g$, so their genera agree. Hence $X=H_g\cup_f(-H_g)$, with $f:\partial H_g\to\partial H_g$ orientation preserving. The identifications are the disk-and-tube constructions just given, not an application of three-manifold classification. By step 9.1, $f$ is smoothly isotopic to a finite twist word.

**Local trace of a twist.** Suppose $Y=H_g\cup_q(-H_g)$ and $c$ is a curve on the splitting surface. Push it into a product collar and let $(\mu,\lambda)$ be the meridian and surface-parallel longitude of a solid-torus neighborhood. Cutting the splitting annulus and regluing by $(\theta,u)\mapsto(\theta\pm2\pi b(u),u)$ adds one signed longitude circuit to a normal meridian. The replacing solid torus therefore has meridian $\mu\pm\lambda$. Conversely this filling cancels the shear, because the coordinate change is identity at the annulus ends. This is integral surgery with coefficient $\pm1$ relative to the surface framing. The sign is chosen to realize the specified twist on the chosen side of the collar. Attaching a four-dimensional two-handle $D^2\times D^2$ to $Y\times[0,1]$ with that framing removes $S^1\times\operatorname{int}D^2$ from the outgoing boundary and inserts $D^2\times S^1$, exactly this torus replacement. Its oriented boundary is $(-Y)\sqcup Y'$, where $Y'$ has gluing $T_c^{\pm1}q$. Seams are product charts and corners are rounded away from the incoming face by [F5].

**Construct the filling.** The double $H_g\cup_{\mathrm{id}}(-H_g)$ bounds the rounded product $H_g\times[0,1]$. Attach the finitely many two-handle traces of step 11.1 for a twist word for $f$. The outgoing boundary is $H_g\cup_f(-H_g)$ up to smooth isotopy of the gluing map. Such an isotopy induces a diffeomorphism of glued manifolds: in a collar use $(x,s)\mapsto(f_{\beta(s)}f_0^{-1}(x),s)$ with $\beta$ constant at its ends, and extend by identity. Composing with step 10.1 gives the required orientation-preserving identification $j:\partial W\to X$. For $g=0$ the starting product is a rounded four-ball, and step 9.1 already handles its sphere gluing map.

**Components and markings.** Components of a manifold are open; compactness gives finitely many components of $X$. Perform step 12.1 with each given orientation and take the finite disjoint union. Empty $X$ uses empty $W$. For an actual capped manifold $X=M\cup C$, pull the marked submanifolds and their common collars back by $j$. The specified cap parametrizations and decorations are then exactly retained. A product collar of $\partial W$ presents their common seam as the prescribed corner between the two boundary faces; no diffeomorphism is extended across a cap or across $W$. This is marked boundary existence, with no extra assertion about relative handle trading.

Every input therefore has a single-copy compact oriented smooth filling, so its class is zero in $\Omega_3^{SO}$ by [F6]. The integral conclusion follows from the constructed filling, without rationalization, integral characteristic-number detection or a stable-stem calculation. AC covers the inherited countable choice and the auxiliary smooth choices; for a set of inputs it can additionally select one filling from each nonempty set of fillings. No canonical or natural selection is asserted. [F6, step 13.1] ∎



The source proof of Li–Watts, Section 3, printed pp.12–16, was read in full; steps 1.1–1.4 adapt its vector-field contraction, add the explicit smooth time normalization and bind its planar prerequisites. The topological Alexander trick in Farb–Margalit, pp.50–51, is not a smooth proof. The portions of that complete author draft actually read were Sections 1.3, 2.2.1, 3.5–3.6 and 4.1–4.2, pp.38–43, 50–51, 81–91 and 93–109. They supply the curve-surgery, twist and point-pushing source arguments; steps 1.2–4.2 supply the smooth all-twists proof and the explicit disk-family and first-jet details locally. Neither finite generation by a specified list of curves nor injectivity of a Birman sequence is assumed. The remaining sections of either complete downloaded source are not claimed read. Steps 10.1–6.2 are the local Heegaard/trace construction from the actual general Morse suppliers and the stated smooth boundary conventions.

Let $M$ be a smooth $m$-manifold and let $0\le p\le m-1$, with $q=m-p$, so
that $q\ge1$. A **framed embedded surgery sphere** of dimension $p$ in $M$ is a
smooth embedding
$$\varphi:S^p\times D^q\hookrightarrow M$$
whose image lies in the interior of $M$. Its **underlying sphere** is the smooth
embedding $\varphi_0:S^p\to M$, $\varphi_0(x)=\varphi(x,0)$ obtained by
restricting to the zero of the disk factor
([[def-smooth-embedding]], [[def-smooth-manifold]]). The differential in the disk directions at $(x,0)$, followed by the quotient
$T_{\varphi_0(x)}M\to T_{\varphi_0(x)}M/d\varphi_0(T_xS^p)$, is a linear
isomorphism $\mathbb R^q\to\nu_{\varphi_0,x}$: $d\varphi$ is invertible and
its sphere directions are precisely the tangent space of the underlying
sphere. These isomorphisms vary smoothly and give its **normal framing**
([[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]).
The framing is
part of the data and is fixed, not taken up to homotopy: the same underlying
sphere with a different trivialization is a different framed embedded surgery
sphere.

The existence of such product-embedding data is equivalent to triviality of
the normal bundle, as proved in the
framing lemma of this page using the tubular neighbourhood theorem. A framing
alone does not specify a unique tubular embedding; here the entire embedding
$\varphi$ is supplied. The
disk-factor convention $D^q$ matches the handle vocabulary of
[[def-k-handle-core-cocore-attaching-region-and-belt-sphere]]: the attaching
region of the standard handle is a product of a sphere and a disk, and its
attaching sphere is the zero of the disk factor.

The range is the one fixed by the plan: $0\le p\le m-1$, equivalently $q\ge1$.
The case $p=m-1$ is included, and then $q=1$: the framing trivializes a normal
line bundle, so the normal direction must be orientable. The case $p=m$ is not
included, because then the disk factor would be $D^0$ and the construction
below would require a surgery on an $S^{-1}$, which is not defined. No
orientation of $M$ is assumed, and the definition performs no construction: an
existence statement for $\varphi$ is not part of it.

The smooth structure and boundary conventions used for $M$ are those of
[[def-smooth-manifold]] and
[[def-smooth-chart-atlas-and-structure-on-a-manifold-with-boundary]], and the
smooth vector bundle conventions are those of
[[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]]. This definition
uses no choice principle.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $M$ be a smooth
$m$-manifold, let $0\le p\le m-1$ and $q=m-p$, so that $q\ge1$, and let
$\varphi:S^p\times D^q\hookrightarrow M$ be a framed embedded surgery sphere
with image in the interior of $M$ ([[def-framed-embedded-surgery-sphere]]). The
**$p$-surgery on $M$ along $\varphi$**, also called a spherical modification of
type $(p+1,q)$, is the smooth $m$-manifold $M_\varphi$ obtained by removing the
open tubular piece $\varphi(S^p\times\operatorname{int}D^q)$ and gluing in
$D^{p+1}\times S^{q-1}$ along the common boundary, using the identification
induced by $\varphi$ on $S^p\times S^{q-1}$:
$$M_\varphi=\bigl(M\setminus\varphi(S^p\times\operatorname{int}D^q)\bigr)\cup_{\varphi|_{S^p\times S^{q-1}}}\bigl(D^{p+1}\times S^{q-1}\bigr).$$

The two pieces are smooth manifolds with boundary sharing the boundary component
$S^p\times S^{q-1}$ under the identification induced by $\varphi$; the complement
also retains $\partial M$. They are glued along collars of the shared component and the seam is
smoothed by the signed collar charts also used along the boundary of a smooth handle attachment
([[def-attaching-a-smooth-handle-with-corner-rounding]],
[[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]]). The smooth structure produced this way is
independent of the auxiliary collar and smoothing choices up to a
diffeomorphism supported near the seam; this is proved by the gluing lemma of
this page, and it is the sense in which the construction is
well defined ([[lem-surgery-gluing-has-a-canonical-smooth-structure-up-to-diffeomorphism]]).

The **core sphere** is $\varphi_0:S^p\to M$, $\varphi_0(x)=\varphi(x,0)$; it
lies in the removed piece and is not a submanifold of $M_\varphi$. The **belt sphere** is
$\{0\}\times S^{q-1}\subseteq
D^{p+1}\times S^{q-1}\subseteq M_\varphi$, a closed embedded $(q-1)$-sphere with
the normal data of the disk-factor decomposition
([[def-k-handle-core-cocore-attaching-region-and-belt-sphere]]). The glued-in
disk factor has dimension $p+1$, while the whole piece has dimension
$(p+1)+(q-1)=m$. The disk dimension is the index shift recorded by the trace
construction of this page.

The boundary identification is the restriction of the supplied product
embedding $\varphi$, whose derivative along the core induces the normal
framing. Changing that embedding or its framing can change the surgery, but
distinct normal framings need not give distinct boundary identifications or
distinct diffeomorphism types. Nothing in the definition
asserts that a framing exists for a given embedded sphere; that condition is the
content of the framing lemma of this page.

When $\partial M\ne\varnothing$ the construction takes place in the interior of
$M$ and leaves $\partial M$ unchanged: the removed piece lies in the interior
and the glued-in piece meets $\partial M$ in no point. The case $p=m-1$ (so $q=1$)
replaces an open product neighbourhood $S^{m-1}\times(-1,1)$ by the two disks
$D^m\times S^0$; the openness of the removed piece and the count of the disk
factors are the point of the endpoint formula, which is computed on the B page.
No case $p=m$ is included, since then $q=0$ and the boundary being traded would
be $S^m\times S^{-1}$; the range $0\le p\le m-1$ excludes it, in accordance with
the plan's binding repair.

The smooth structure and boundary conventions are those of
[[def-smooth-chart-atlas-and-structure-on-a-manifold-with-boundary]], and
diffeomorphism means diffeomorphism of smooth manifolds
([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]). Countable Choice
is used exactly where the cited collar and handle-attachment suppliers use it,
that is, in the existence of the collars along which the two pieces are glued.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $N$ be a smooth
$n$-manifold with boundary, let $0\le k\le n$, and let
$N'=N\cup_\psi h^k$ be obtained by attaching the standard $k$-handle
$D^k\times D^{n-k}$ along an embedding
$\psi:S^{k-1}\times D^{n-k}\to\partial N$ that extends over a neighbourhood of
the disk factor, with corners rounded. Then:

(i) $\partial(D^k\times D^{n-k})=(S^{k-1}\times D^{n-k})\cup(D^k\times S^{n-k-1})$
with intersection $S^{k-1}\times S^{n-k-1}$;

(ii) the boundary of $N'$ is obtained from $\partial N$ by trading the open
attaching region for the outgoing region,
$$\partial N'\cong\bigl(\partial N\setminus\psi(S^{k-1}\times\operatorname{int}D^{n-k})\bigr)\cup_{\psi|_{S^{k-1}\times S^{n-k-1}}}\bigl(D^k\times S^{n-k-1}\bigr),$$
the identification on the overlap being $\psi$;

(iii) the belt sphere $\{0\}\times S^{n-k-1}$ is a closed embedded submanifold of
$\partial N'$, and its normal bundle in $\partial N'$ is identified with the
bundle of $D^k$-factor directions.

Endpoint cases: for $k=0$ the attaching region is empty and
$\partial N'=\partial N\sqcup S^{n-1}$; for $k=n$ the outgoing region is empty
and the attaching region is the sphere $S^{n-1}\times D^0$, which the handle
$D^n\times D^0$ caps.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $M$ be a smooth
$m$-manifold, $0\le p\le m-1$, $q=m-p$, and let $\varphi$ be a framed embedded
surgery sphere in $M$. Write
$N=M\setminus\varphi(S^p\times\operatorname{int}D^q)$ for the complement of the
open tubular piece. Then:

(i) $N$ and $D^{p+1}\times S^{q-1}$ are smooth manifolds sharing the boundary component
$S^p\times S^{q-1}$ under the identification induced by $\varphi$, and gluing
them along collars of this common boundary, with the seam smoothed in the
standard way, gives a smooth $m$-manifold $M_\varphi$ without new boundary when
$M$ is closed, respectively with boundary $\partial M$ in general;

(ii) any two collar systems and compatible smoothings give smooth structures
related by a diffeomorphism equal to the identity outside an arbitrarily small
neighbourhood of the seam;

(iii) if $\varphi_t$ is a smooth isotopy of framed embeddings of
$S^p\times D^q$ into $\operatorname{int}M$, constant for $t$ near $0$ and $1$,
then $M_{\varphi_0}$ and $M_{\varphi_1}$ are diffeomorphic by a
diffeomorphism supported near the swept region.

Consequently the diffeomorphism type of the $p$-surgery depends only on the
isotopy class of the framed embedding, and the construction of the definition
is unambiguous up to diffeomorphism.

For fixed attaching and product-collar data, two compatible smooth monotone roundings of a handle attachment are diffeomorphic by an isotopy supported in that collar. The diffeomorphism is the identity outside the collar.

derivations.claim: **Product exterior and actual slopes.** Use the abstract product coordinates of $N$ to draw it as an unknotted solid torus in $S^3$. Let $A$ be the core of the complementary solid torus. Then $K$ is linked once with $A$ and $U$, while $A,U$ are disjoint meridians of $K$. The exterior of $A\cup K\cup U$ is  $X=P\times S^1,$  where $P$ is a disk with two disjoint interior disks removed. One way to see this product without a diagram is to remove $K$ first: its exterior in $S^3$ is $D^2\times S^1$, where the circle factor is the meridian of $K$; the two meridians $A,U$ are fibers $\{a\}\times S^1$ and $\{u\}\times S^1$. Removing their product tubular neighborhoods removes two disks from the first factor. The boundary tori are $T_K,T_A,T_U$, corresponding to the three boundary circles of $P$.  Write $h$ for the positive product fiber and $b_K,b_A,b_U$ for the three oriented base-boundary circles. In the usual meridian/longitude coordinates,  $\mu_K=h,\quad\lambda_K=b_K,\qquad\mu_U=b_U,\quad\lambda_U=h.$  The retained external torus is $T_A$; its solid-torus meridian in the original $N$ is $h$. Thus the two filling slopes are $b_K+fh$ and $h$, where $f$ is the integer framing on $K$ relative to the selected product longitude. All these are identifications of actual product annuli and circles; no homology-only recognition of a filled manifold is being used.

**Framing reduction relative to the retained torus.** There is a smooth map $\xi:P\to S^1$ of degree $f$ on the $K$ boundary, degree $-f$ on the $U$ boundary (with the common oriented-boundary convention), and constant one on a collar of the $A$ boundary. Explicitly draw $P$ as a planar disk punctured at $a,u$, start with $((z-u)/|z-u|)^f$, and modify it on a collar of the $A$ boundary to be one. Its winding number there is zero, so it has a smooth real argument on that collar; multiply by the inverse argument with a collar cutoff. This changes no boundary degrees. Choose the boundary collar arguments similarly to make the restrictions standard rotations in their angular coordinates. The map  $\Phi:X\to X,\qquad\Phi(x,t)=(x,\xi(x)t)$  is an explicit diffeomorphism, the identity on $T_A$, fixing $h$ and sending $b_K$ to $b_K+fh$. On $T_U$ it also preserves the filling slope $h$. It extends over the $U$ filling: a solid torus whose meridian is $h$ admits the explicit extension of the boundary map $b_U\mapsto b_U-fh$, $h\mapsto h$ obtained by rotating its meridian disk by $-f$ turns as its longitude runs once. In coordinates $(re^{i\theta},e^{i\varphi})$ this is $(re^{i(\theta-f\varphi)},e^{i\varphi})$. Constants or zero-degree boundary phase changes extend by the same collar interpolation. Hence it suffices to prove the identity for the pair of slopes $b_K,h$. Equivalently one can choose the product framing on $N$ to agree with the supplied framing of $K$ from the outset; conjugating a boundary-relative diffeomorphism by that product identification is still boundary-relative.

**The proper disk and the cut-open compression body.** Fill $T_U$ with a solid torus $V=D^2\times S^1$ whose meridian $\partial D^2\times\{1\}$ is identified with $h$. Choose an embedded base arc $\alpha$ from the $A$ boundary to the $U$ boundary, disjoint from the $K$ boundary. The vertical annulus $\alpha\times S^1\subset X$ has a fiber boundary on each of $T_A,T_U$. Cap its $T_U$ boundary by the displayed meridian disk of $V$. After rounding its one seam, this is an embedded proper disk $D$ with boundary $h\subset T_A$.  The cut-open manifold $(X\cup V)\setminus\!\setminus D$ is a punctured solid torus whose uncompressed torus boundary is $T_K$ and whose meridian there is $h$. Here is the cut-and-glue verification. Cut $P$ along $\alpha$; it becomes an annulus. Consequently the product cut along the vertical annulus is an annulus times $S^1$, namely $T^2\times I$. Cutting $V$ along its meridian disk gives $D^2\times I$. Its annular attaching face is $\partial D^2\times I$, attached in the $h$ direction of the boundary created from the $A/U$ sides of the cut. Thus the cut-open manifold is exactly $T^2\times I$ with one 3-dimensional 2-handle $D^2\times I$ attached along the primitive curve $h$ on one of its ends. That end compresses to a sphere, while the other end remains $T_K$.  This compression body is $(D^2\times S^1)\setminus\operatorname{int}B^3$ with meridian $h$: in the explicit product solid torus, take a meridian disk $D^2\times\{1\}$, thicken it, and retain a boundary collar. Their union is the just-described $T^2\times I$ plus the meridian 2-handle. The complementary region is the interior of the product obtained by cutting the solid torus along that meridian disk, hence is a 3-ball. This identifies the compression body by its actual collar and disk, rather than inferring its type from its fundamental group. The compressed sphere consists of the original annular part of $T_A$ and the two copies of $D$, with their product attaching coordinates retained.

**The remaining filling and boundary reconstruction.** Now fill $T_K$ along $b_K$. Its filling meridian intersects the compression body's meridian $h$ once. The filled, punctured solid torus is therefore a 3-ball. Explicitly, the unpunctured union is the boundary of $D^2\times D^2$: the pieces $D^2\times S^1$ and $S^1\times D^2$ are its two solid tori, and their meridians are the two product circle factors $h,b_K$. Thus it is $S^3$ with its explicit standard product smoothing. Retaining the already specified puncture removes an ordinary product ball from that standard sphere and leaves a ball, with the annular boundary part inherited from $T_A$ and the two disk faces inherited from $D$.  Finally restore the cut along $D$. This attaches one ordinary 3-dimensional 1-handle to that ball, along the two displayed disk faces. It is a solid torus. Its meridian disk is $D$, so its external meridian is exactly $h$. More precisely the ball-with-two-disk-faces just constructed has its remaining annular boundary in the original $T_A$ product coordinates; regluing these two product disk faces reconstructs the same $D^2\times S^1$ product neighborhood with the same annular side. Choose the product ball and the meridian disk in the original $N$ by cutting its specified meridian disk. The preceding product identifications match those cut coordinates and their annular side. They therefore give a diffeomorphism after regluing whose restriction to all of $T_A$ is the original identity. No arbitrary boundary diffeomorphism is discarded or extended by a classification theorem. Compatible corner smoothings are compared in their seam collars by the existing rounding lemma.  Combining this boundary-relative identification with the explicit framing-reduction map $\Phi$ proves the Statement for every integral $f$.
