citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Every compact closed oriented smooth one-manifold is the oriented boundary of a compact smooth oriented two-manifold. Every compact closed oriented smooth two-manifold is the oriented boundary of a compact smooth oriented three-manifold. Empty and disconnected inputs are included. Consequently $\Omega^{SO}_1=\Omega^{SO}_2=0$ integrally.

Assume AC. Every compact closed oriented smooth three-manifold $X$ admits a compact oriented smooth four-manifold $W$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $j:\partial W\to X$. Disconnected and empty manifolds are included. Consequently $\Omega_3^{SO}=0$ integrally, with a single copy of each input manifold.

More precisely, if $X=M\cup C$ is an actual closed manifold obtained by attaching specified smooth caps $C$ to a compact oriented three-manifold $M$ along specified collared boundary parametrizations, the identification $j$ retains these marked submanifolds, their parametrizations and any decorations by pullback. No extension of a boundary diffeomorphism across a cap or filling is required. The assertion is existence; a simultaneous choice of fillings for a set of inputs may use AC and is not asserted canonical.

Assume AC, used only through embeddings, tubular neighbourhoods, approximation
and classifying maps. For every $n\ge0$ the collapse construction induces
isomorphisms of abelian groups
$$\Omega_n^{O}\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\pi_n(M\mathrm O),\qquad \Omega_n^{SO}\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\pi_n(M\mathrm{SO}),$$
where the right-hand sides are the stable homotopy groups of the Thom
prespectra of the universal real and oriented bundles. A collapse at any sufficiently large embedding rank represents the stable
image, and the inverse sends a class represented by a map transverse to the zero section to
the unoriented bordism class of the preimage with its pulled-back normal bundle,
with the orientation-induced refinement in the oriented case. The isomorphisms
are compatible with disjoint union, with products, and with null-cobordism in
that a null-cobordant manifold has zero stable class.

Assume AC. For every integer $n\ge8$ and any CW model $K(\mathbb Z,n)$,
$$H_{n+5}(K(\mathbb Z,n);\mathbb Z)=0.$$

Assume AC. Let R be a nonzero commutative unital ring with 2 invertible. For m≥1, H*(BSO(2m+1);R)=R[p₁,…,p_m], H*(BSO(2m);R)=R[p₁,…,p_{m−1},e] with p_m=e², and H*(BO(2m);R)=H*(BO(2m+1);R)=R[p₁,…,p_m]. The indicated generators are the actual universal Euler and Pontryagin classes, |e|=2m and |p_i|=4i. Orientation reversal fixes p_i and negates e. BSO(1) has cohomology R in degree zero only, BO(1) likewise, and rank zero is a point. The chosen BSO(r) is the lifted Schubert CW model.

Assume AC. For every $n\geq0$,
$$H^*(B\operatorname O(n);\mathbb F_2)=\mathbb F_2[w_1,\ldots,w_n],\qquad |w_i|=i,$$
where $B\operatorname O(n)=\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb R^\infty)$ is the
stable real Grassmannian and $w_i=w_i(\gamma_n)$ are the Stiefel–Whitney
classes of its tautological bundle. For $n=0$ the right side is $\mathbb F_2$.

Assume AC.  For an $R$-oriented rank-$n$ bundle $\xi$ in the scope of the
general Thom theorem, including $n=0$, there is a natural exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^{k-n}(B;R)\xrightarrow{\smile e_{\rm Th}(\xi)}H^k(B;R)\xrightarrow{p^*}H^k(S(\xi);R)\xrightarrow{\partial_G}H^{k-n+1}(B;R)\xrightarrow{\smile e_{\rm Th}(\xi)}\cdots.$$
For $n\geq2$, with the preceding cohomological Serre convention, the Euler
class is the transgression $d_n$ of the normalized generator of
$H^{n-1}(S^{n-1};R)$.  Ranks zero and one are covered by the pair sequence,
but not by that path-connected-sphere Serre comparison.

Assume AC, inherited from the cited bundle, cohomology, or operation suppliers. For n≥1, the forgetful map Gr⁺_n(R∞)=BSO(n)→Gr_n(R∞)=BO(n) is a two-sheeted cover, including n=1, where it is S∞→RP∞. Each Schubert cell has exactly two lifted cells, and these cells give BSO(n) the CW weak topology with finite boundary support. Set BSO(0) to the point.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ be a numerable real vector bundle of rank $n\geq0$
over a paracompact Hausdorff CGWH base of CW homotopy type, and let
$q:\operatorname{Fl}(E)\to B$ be its real flag bundle. Then
$\operatorname{Fl}(E)$ is a base of the same kind,
$$q^*E\cong L_1\oplus\cdots\oplus L_n\qquad\text{over }\operatorname{Fl}(E),$$
and the pullback
$$q^*:H^*(B;\mathbb F_2)\longrightarrow H^*(\operatorname{Fl}(E);\mathbb F_2)$$
is injective. Moreover, finitely many numerable real bundles
$E_1,\ldots,E_m$ over $B$ admit a common paracompact Hausdorff CGWH base of
CW homotopy type
$X\to B$ with $X=\operatorname{Fl}(E_1)\times_B\cdots\times_B
\operatorname{Fl}(E_m)$ over which every $q^*E_k$ splits as a sum of line
bundles and whose projection $X\to B$ induces an injection on
$\mathbb F_2$-cohomology.

For $x\in H^p(X;\mathbb F_2)$, $y\in H^q(X;\mathbb F_2)$, and every integer
$k$, the Steenrod squares satisfy the Cartan formula

$$
Sq^k(x\smile y)=\sum_{i+j=k}Sq^i(x)\smile Sq^j(y).
$$

Only finitely many terms are nonzero. More generally, for classes on two
spaces the external formula is

$$
Sq^k(x\times y)=\sum_{i+j=k}Sq^i(x)\times Sq^j(y).
$$

For $x\in H^n(X;\mathbb F_2)$,

$$
Sq^0x=x,\qquad Sq^k x=0\ \text{if }k>n,\qquad Sq^n x=x\smile x.
$$

The same assertions hold relatively. On reduced cohomology of based CW
complexes, every square commutes with the standard cohomology suspension:

$$
Sq^k(\sigma x)=\sigma(Sq^k x).
$$

For the integral Bockstein
$\beta_{\mathbb Z}:H^n(X;\mathbb F_2)\to H^{n+1}(X;\mathbb Z)$ of the coefficient
sequence $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb F_2\to0$, reduction
modulo two satisfies
$$\rho_2\beta_{\mathbb Z}(x)=Sq^1(x)$$
for every space $X$, every $n\geq0$ and every $x\in H^n(X;\mathbb F_2)$. No
choice principle is needed.

Assume AC. For every space $X$, abelian group $G$ and $n\ge0$ there is a natural short exact sequence
$$0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathbb Z}(H_{n-1}(X;\mathbb Z),G)\xrightarrow{\iota}H^n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\beta}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(H_n(X;\mathbb Z),G)\longrightarrow0.$$
The same assertion holds with $(X,A)$ in every homology and cohomology term for any subspace $A\subseteq X$. Here $H_{-1}=0$ and Ext is computed from projective resolutions of the first variable, with the comparison identifications proved in the local extension lemma. The map $\beta$ is evaluation. Naturality is contravariant in continuous maps of spaces or pairs and covariant in coefficient homomorphisms.

Every finitely generated abelian group $G$ has unique canonical decompositions

$$G\cong\mathbb Z^r\oplus\mathbb Z/(n_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathbb Z/(n_t),\qquad 1<n_1\mid\cdots\mid n_t,$$

and

$$G\cong\mathbb Z^r\oplus\bigoplus_{p,j}\mathbb Z/(p^{e_{p,j}}),$$

where $r$ and the finite torsion data are unique up to the stated order. The torsion summand is finite. The trivial group has $r=0$ and empty torsion data.

Assume AC and let $n\ge2$. In the oriented Grassmannian model $B_n=\operatorname{Gr}_n^+(\mathbb R^\infty)$ let $\gamma_n^+\to B_n$ be the tautological oriented bundle with its Euclidean metric, and put $S_n=S(\gamma_n^+)$ with projection $p:S_n\to B_n$.

1. The actual sphere bundle $S^{n-1}\to S_n\xrightarrow{p}B_n$ is a Hurewicz fibration. The complement map
$$r:S_n\longrightarrow B_{n-1},\qquad (V,o,v)\longmapsto v^\perp\cap V$$
is a homotopy equivalence. Orient its target plane $W=v^\perp\cap V$ so that $(v,w_1,\ldots,w_{n-1})$ is positive in $(V,o)$ whenever $(w_1,\ldots,w_{n-1})$ is positive in $W$. Thus the notation $S^{n-1}\to B\operatorname{SO}(n-1)\to B\operatorname{SO}(n)$ denotes this fibration with a homotopy-equivalent model for its total space, not a literal replacement by a homeomorphic Grassmannian.
2. On the actual total space, the orientation-preserving ordered splitting is
$$p^*\gamma_n^+\cong\varepsilon^1\oplus r^*\gamma_{n-1}^+,$$
where the positive generator of the first summand is the tautological unit vector $v$. Interchanging the two factors changes the ordered orientation by $(-1)^{n-1}$.
3. With integral coefficients, $p^*e(\gamma_n^+)=0$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $(X,A)$ be an $(n-1)$-connected CW pair with $A\ne\varnothing$ and supplied characteristic maps. There are, without any choice principle, a CW complex $Z$ containing the given $A$ as a subcomplex, with no cells of $Z\setminus A$ below dimension $n$, and a weak homotopy equivalence $Q:Z\to X$ satisfying $Q|_A=\mathrm{id}_A$.

Assuming the Axiom of Choice, this $Q$ is a homotopy equivalence rel $A$: there is $R:X\to Z$ equal to the identity on $A$, with $RQ\simeq\mathrm{id}_Z$ and $QR\simeq\mathrm{id}_X$ through homotopies fixing $A$ pointwise. Choice is used to produce these homotopies, not to construct the weak model.

Let $(X,x_0)$ be a based CW complex that is $(n-1)$-connected, where $n\ge1$. Let $\Sigma X=C_+X\cup_X C_-X$ be its unreduced two-cone suspension, based at the lower cone point $p_-$. The suspension homomorphism
$$E:\pi_i(X,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_{i+1}(\Sigma X,p_-),\qquad [h]\longmapsto[\Sigma h],$$
where the source sphere is also suspended by the two-cone construction and based at its lower cone point, is an isomorphism for $1\le i<2n-1$ and a surjection for $i=2n-1$. In degree zero both $\pi_0(X)$ and $\pi_1(\Sigma X)$ are singletons, so the corresponding pointed map is a bijection. The theorem and these precise basepoint conventions require no choice principle. No endpoint injectivity is asserted.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair with $A\ne\varnothing$ and supplied characteristic maps. The ordinary quotient $X/A$ is a CW complex, with one vertex $*$ replacing $A$ and one cell of the same dimension for every cell of $X\setminus A$.

If $A$ admits a contraction $H:A\times I\to A$, $H(-,0)=\mathrm{id}_A$, $H(-,1)=a\in A$, then the quotient map $q:X\to X/A$ is a homotopy equivalence and a weak homotopy equivalence. If $H(a,t)=a$ for every $t$, the constructed inverse and inverse homotopies are based at $a$ and $*$. No choice principle is required; a contraction is one witness, not a family of selected contractions.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be paracompact Hausdorff and let
$H:X\times I\to Y$ be a homotopy from $f_0$ to $f_1$. For every numerable
finite-rank real or complex vector bundle $E\to Y$, the endpoint pullbacks
$f_0^*E$ and $f_1^*E$ are isomorphic. Equivalently, the restrictions of
$H^*E$ to $X\times\{0\}$ and $X\times\{1\}$ are isomorphic. No canonical
endpoint isomorphism is asserted.

Assume AC.  Every $R$-oriented rank-$n$ numerable vector bundle over a CW
complex, or over a paracompact Hausdorff base of CW type, has a unique
normalized Thom class $u_\xi$, and
$$a\longmapsto\pi^*a\smile u_\xi:H^k(B;R)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^{k+n}(D(\xi),S(\xi);R)$$
for every $k$.  Without a supplied orientation, the canonical twisted form is
$$H^k(B;\mathcal O_R(\xi))\xrightarrow{\cong}H^{k+n}(D(\xi),S(\xi);R).$$
The finite supplied-trivializing-cover theorem is a choice-free special case.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ be a numerable real vector bundle of rank $n\geq0$
over a paracompact Hausdorff CGWH base of CW type (the admissible bases of this page), with its canonical $\mathbb F_2$-orientation and
normalized mod-two Thom class
$u_E\in H^n(D(E),S(E);\mathbb F_2)$. Then
$$Sq(u_E)=w(E)\smile u_E,$$
equivalently
$$Sq^i(u_E)=w_i(E)\smile u_E\quad\text{for every }i\geq0,$$
with both sides vanishing for $i>n$.

Assume AC. Let $A$ be an abelian group, $n\geq1$, and let $K=K(A,n)$ be a based CW model with its specified isomorphism $\pi_n(K)\cong A$. There is a unique fundamental class

$$ \iota\in H^n(K;A) $$

whose Kronecker evaluation corresponds to $\operatorname{id}_A$ under Hurewicz. For every based CW complex $(X,x_0)$ whose basepoint is a vertex, pullback gives a natural bijection

$$ [X,K]_*\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\widetilde H^n(X;A),\qquad [f]\longmapsto f^*\iota, $$

where $\widetilde H^n(X;A)=H^n(X,\{x_0\};A)$. Since $n>0$, the map from relative to absolute cohomology identifies this group with $H^n(X;A)$ whenever $X$ is connected, and in fact componentwise for every nonempty $X$.

Every continuous $f:X\to Y$ factors as $f=p_fj_f$, where $j_f:X\to E_f$ is a homotopy equivalence and $p_f:E_f\to Y$ is a Hurewicz fibration. This holds for all ordinary spaces and, with the specified kified constructions, in CGWH. No surjectivity onto components disjoint from $f(X)$ is asserted. The result is choice-free.

For a based Serre fibration $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ with fiber $F=p^{-1}(b_0)$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to\pi_n(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_n(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_n(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_{n-1}(F)\to\cdots\to\pi_1(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_0(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_0(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_0(B)$$
is exact wherever there is an incoming and outgoing arrow. Basepoints are $e_0,b_0$ as appropriate. Exactness means incoming image equals the inverse image of the distinguished element. Arrows are homomorphisms where both group structures are defined; the component terms are pointed sets. The last arrow is onto precisely when $p(E)$ meets every path component of $B$.

There is a right action of $\pi_1(B,b_0)$ on $\pi_0(F)$: $[e]\cdot[\gamma]$ is the endpoint component of a lift of $\gamma$ starting at $e$, with loop products traversed left-to-right. Its orbits are precisely the fibers of $i_*:\pi_0(F)\to\pi_0(E)$, and the stabilizer of $[e_0]$ is $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$. Our boundary convention gives $\partial_p[\gamma]=[e_0]\cdot[\gamma]^{-1}$. These assertions require no AC.

Let $n\ge2$ and assume the Axiom of Choice. If a CW complex $X$ is $(n-1)$-connected, then for every $x\in X$
$$\widetilde H_i(X;\mathbb Z)=0\quad(0\le i<n),\qquad h:\pi_n(X,x)\xrightarrow{\cong}H_n(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The same conclusion holds for an $(n-1)$-connected space already known to be homotopy equivalent to a CW complex, using an actual homotopy equivalence.

Separately, for $n=1$ and any nonempty path-connected space $X$, the map $h:\pi_1(X,x)\to H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ is the abelianization map: it is surjective with kernel the commutator subgroup, and $\widetilde H_0(X;\mathbb Z)=0$. This degree-one assertion is choice-free and requires no CW-type assumption. A bare weak CW approximation is not the hypothesis used for the CW-type transfer above.

For every topological space $X$ there are a CW complex $\Gamma X$ and a continuous map $\gamma:\Gamma X\to X$ that induces a bijection on path components and isomorphisms $\pi_n(\Gamma X,z)\to\pi_n(X,\gamma(z))$ for every $z\in\Gamma X$ and every $n\ge1$.

More generally, given a CW complex $P$ with supplied structure and a continuous map $q:P\to X$, there are a CW complex $Z$ containing $P$ as a subcomplex and a map $Q:Z\to X$ extending $q$ with those same weak-equivalence properties. In particular, for a pair $(X,A)$ a prescribed CW approximation $q_A:P\to A$ extends to a map of pairs $(Z,P)\to(X,A)$ whose map on the whole spaces is a CW approximation of $X$ and whose restriction is exactly $q_A$.

No choice principle is assumed. Cells are indexed by all actual maps and extension data, not by a selected set of homotopy-class representatives. Only the finite-source clause of cellular approximation is used. No separation or compact-generation assumption is placed on $X$.

Every weak homotopy equivalence $f:X\to Y$ of topological spaces induces isomorphisms $H_k(X;\mathbb Z)\to H_k(Y;\mathbb Z)$ for all $k\ge0$, without any choice principle. More generally, if $A\subseteq X$, $B\subseteq Y$, $f(A)\subseteq B$, and both $f$ and $f|_A:A\to B$ are weak homotopy equivalences, then the induced maps $H_k(X,A;\mathbb Z)\to H_k(Y,B;\mathbb Z)$ are isomorphisms. No separation or CW hypothesis is imposed on these spaces.

Let $p:E\to B$ be a Serre fibration over a path-connected CW complex and
let $R$ be a commutative unital ring. The skeletal filtration gives a
choice-free natural first-quadrant homological spectral sequence
$$E^2_{a,b}\cong H_a\bigl(B;\mathcal H_b(p;R)\bigr), \qquad d_r:E^r_{a,b}\longrightarrow E^r_{a-r,b+r-1},$$
strongly converging to $H_{a+b}(E;R)$ with the finite image filtration
$$F_aH_n(E;R)=\operatorname{im}\bigl(H_n(E_a;R)\to H_n(E;R)\bigr), \qquad 0=F_{-1}H_n\subseteq\cdots\subseteq F_nH_n=H_n(E;R).$$
Its stable terms have the specified natural identifications
$$E^\infty_{a,n-a}\cong F_aH_n(E;R)/F_{a-1}H_n(E;R).$$
If $B$ is simply connected, transport between two fiber stalks is independent
of the path class, so after choosing one fiber identification the local
system is constant. The displayed spectral sequence then has
$E^2_{a,b}\cong H_a(B;H_b(F;R))$.

The chain filtration itself is not asserted to be degreewise finite. Strong
convergence follows from the argument below, not from the theorem for
degreewise finite filtered chain complexes.

Assume AC, inherited from Poincare-Lefschetz duality. Let $W$ be a compact
oriented smooth $(4k+1)$-manifold with boundary $M=\partial W$ carrying the
induced orientation and inclusion $i:M\hookrightarrow W$. Then $\sigma(M)=0$.
Consequently, if $M_0,M_1$ are closed oriented $4k$-manifolds that are oriented
cobordant ([[def-oriented-smooth-cobordism]]), then
$\sigma(M_0)=\sigma(M_1)$: by [[def-oriented-smooth-cobordism]],
$\partial V=(-M_0)\sqcup M_1$; reversing the orientation of $V$ gives
$\partial(-V)=M_0\sqcup(-M_1)$ as an oriented boundary, so
$0=\sigma(M_0\sqcup(-M_1))=\sigma(M_0)-\sigma(M_1)$ by
[[lem-signature-is-additive-under-disjoint-union-and-orientation-reversal]].
Hence $\sigma$ descends to a well-defined additive map on oriented bordism
classes $\Omega_{4k}^{SO}\to\mathbb Z$ and vanishes on null-cobordant classes
([[def-null-cobordant-closed-manifold]]).

Assume AC, inherited from the signature form and L-genus suppliers. For every
$k\ge0$, with the complex orientation of $\mathbb{CP}^{2k}$,
$$\sigma(\mathbb{CP}^{2k})=1=L[\mathbb{CP}^{2k}].$$

Assume AC, inherited from the rational spanning proposition. Let $M$ and $N$ be
closed oriented $n$-manifolds. Then $M$ and $N$ are equal in
$\Omega_n^{SO}\otimes\mathbb Q$ if and only if all of their Pontryagin numbers
agree. Equivalently, the map
$$\Omega_n^{SO}\otimes\mathbb Q\longrightarrow \prod_{J}\mathbb Q,\qquad [M]\otimes1\longmapsto \bigl(p_{J}[M]\bigr)_{J},$$
is injective; it is an isomorphism after restricting to the finitely many
partitions $J$ of $n/4$ when $4\mid n$, and both sides are zero when
$4\nmid n$. In particular, if all Pontryagin numbers of a closed oriented
manifold vanish, then some positive multiple of it is an oriented boundary. The
statement is rational only; the integral refinement with Stiefel-Whitney
numbers is Wall's theorem, recorded separately.

Assume AC. For every abelian group A, A⊗_Z Q is its positive-integer localization: every element is a/s and a/s=0 iff a is killed by some positive integer. Thus A⊗Q=0 iff A is torsion. Rationalization is exact and commutes with direct sums. Naturally for every space Y, H_j(Y;Z)⊗Q≅H_j(Y;Q); for every rational vector space V, H_j(Y;V)≅H_j(Y;Q)⊗_Q V.

Fix $n\ge0$. By the cobordism equivalence relation
([[thm-smooth-cobordism-is-an-equivalence-relation]]) the closed smooth
$n$-manifolds are partitioned into cobordism classes
([[def-unoriented-smooth-cobordism-of-closed-manifolds]]). Let
$$\Omega_n^{O}:=\{\,[M]\;:\;M\ \text{a closed smooth }n\text{-manifold}\,\}$$
be the set of these classes in the bounded model convention below, and let
$$\Omega_n^{SO}:=\{\,[Q,o]\;:\;(Q,o)\ \text{a closed oriented smooth }n\text{-manifold}\,\}$$
be the set of oriented cobordism classes
([[def-oriented-smooth-cobordism]]).

**Set-size convention.** For each $n$ use the set of all closed smooth
$n$-manifold structures on subsets of $U_n=\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb N$,
and in the oriented theory include the orientation datum, before taking the
quotient by cobordism. Every closed smooth $n$-manifold has such a model:
compactness gives a finite chart cover $(V_j,\varphi_j)_{j<k}$, and the map
$x\mapsto(\varphi_j(x),j)$, with $j$ the least index for which $x\in V_j$,
is injective into $U_n$. Transport the topology, maximal atlas, and supplied
orientation along this injection; its image is diffeomorphic to the original
manifold. This uses only a finite chart cover, not a choice of a model for every
manifold simultaneously. Two transported models are diffeomorphic, and a
cylinder of [[lem-cylinders-give-reflexivity-of-cobordism]] with outgoing
collar composed with a diffeomorphism's inverse shows they are cobordant (orientation-preservingly in the oriented case). Thus $[M]$
means the unique class of any such model. Products and disjoint unions are
returned to this set of models in the same way; their class is independent of
the transport.

**The operation.** Disjoint union of manifolds defines operations
$$[M]+[N]:=[M\sqcup N]\quad\text{on }\Omega_n^{O},\qquad [Q,o]+[R,p]:=[Q\sqcup R,\,o\sqcup p]\quad\text{on }\Omega_n^{SO},$$
where $o\sqcup p$ is the orientation of the disjoint union whose restriction to
each summand is the given orientation, and finite disjoint unions carry the transported component atlases
([[prop-countable-disjoint-unions-of-fixed-dimensional-smooth-manifolds-are-smooth-manifolds]]);
for summands with boundary the same construction uses half-space charts.
Finite union preserves compactness and combines finitely many countable bases,
so this boundary extension requires no countable choice.
The class of the empty $n$-manifold is the displayed **zero** $0$: it is
null-cobordant and is a two-sided identity for the operation, since
$M\sqcup\varnothing$ is canonically diffeomorphic to $M$
([[def-null-cobordant-closed-manifold]]).

**Well-definedness.** The operations are independent of the chosen
representatives. If $W_i$ is a bordism from $M_i$ to $M_i'$ for $i=0,1$, then
the disjoint union $W_0\sqcup W_1$ carries the canonical smooth structure of a
compact $(n+1)$-manifold with boundary
$\partial(W_0\sqcup W_1)=(\partial W_0)\sqcup(\partial W_1)$, the collars
$\theta_0^0\sqcup\theta_0^1$ and $\theta_1^0\sqcup\theta_1^1$ are smooth
embeddings onto collar neighbourhoods of the boundary parts, and the
decomposition of the boundary into the two parts is again open and closed;
hence $W_0\sqcup W_1$ is a bordism from $M_0\sqcup M_1$ to
$M_0'\sqcup M_1'$. In the oriented case, orienting the disjoint union by the
given orientations makes the disjoint union of the oriented bordisms an
oriented bordism between the disjoint unions, because the induced boundary
orientation is computed componentwise and each summand carries its required
sign. Thus $[M_0\sqcup M_1]=[M_0'\sqcup M_1']$ whenever $[M_i]=[M_i']$, and
similarly in the oriented theory. The class of a finite disjoint union is
computed from the canonical smooth structure on disjoint unions; no further
choice is made.

**Deferred axioms and the forgetful map.** That these operations satisfy the
group axioms (associativity, commutativity, identity and inverses) is not
asserted here: it is proved in the following theorem, together with the
finiteness of the inverse in the unoriented theory. The **forgetful map**
$$\Omega_n^{SO}\longrightarrow\Omega_n^{O},\qquad [Q,o]\longmapsto[Q],$$
sends the oriented class of a closed oriented $n$-manifold to its underlying
unoriented cobordism class; it is well defined because an oriented bordism
between two oriented manifolds is in particular a bordism between their
underlying manifolds, so oriented cobordant manifolds are cobordant.

derivations.claim: Fix $q\ge8$. The determinant-line sphere bundle over $BO(q)$ is its orientation double cover $BSO(q)$. Its mod-two Gysin sequence has multiplication by $w_1$ as its Euler map. This multiplication is injective in the polynomial ring of [F3], so pullback gives $H^*(BSO(q);\mathbb F_2)=\mathbb F_2[w_2,\ldots,w_q]$. This uses the canonical mod-two orientation of the line bundle, rather than assuming it is integrally oriented. The same space has degreewise finitely generated integral homology by its lifted Schubert cells. It is simply connected: the universal oriented-frame bundle has contractible total space and connected fiber $SO(q)$, so its component sequence gives $\pi_1BSO(q)=0$. The frame-bundle description and connectedness also follow from the actual sphere-bundle induction starting with the contractible $BSO(1)$.

Let $T_q$ be the Thom space of the universal oriented $q$-plane bundle. Its Thom cells are shifted up by $q$. Their integral cellular boundary is the base cellular boundary shifted by $q$: over an adjacent pair of base characteristic disks the fiber orientation is preserved, so the incidence degree is the base incidence degree multiplied by the fixed oriented fiber degree one. With the fiber-first convention this also identifies evaluation of $w_4\bar u_q$ on a shifted homology class with evaluation of $w_4$ on the base class. Hence $H_{q+j}(T_q;\mathbb Z)=H_j(BSO(q);\mathbb Z)$, compatibly with mod-two reduction and evaluation. In particular it is $(q-1)$-connected with $H_q(T_q;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ on the normalized fiber generator. The stabilization $BSO(q)\to BSO(q+1)$ is $q$-connected by the sphere fibration in [F5] and its homotopy sequence. A relative CW model therefore has no new cells of dimension at most $q$. Over each relative characteristic disk trivialize the pulled-back $(q+1)$-plane bundle; its Thom cell has dimension the disk dimension plus $q+1$. This proves that $\Sigma T_q\to T_{q+1}$ has no relative cells below $2q+2$, hence is an isomorphism on homotopy through $2q$. The construction uses a mapping-cylinder relative model and bundle homotopy transport, so it does not assume that particular Grassmannian Schubert structures form a literal relative cell inclusion.

With mod-two splitting roots $t_j$ of degree one, $Sq^1t_j=t_j^2$ and Cartan makes $Sq^1$ a derivation. Expand the elementary symmetric functions: in $w_1w_k$, the terms in which the extra root lies in the chosen $k$-subset are precisely $Sq^1w_k$; every $(k+1)$-subset occurs $k+1$ times among the other terms. Hence $Sq^1w_k=w_1w_k+(k-1)w_{k+1}$. On $BSO(q)$ this gives $Sq^1w_2=w_3$ and $Sq^1w_4=w_5$, both nonzero by step 1.1.

Freudenthal applies to the $(q-1)$-connected Thom CW space and gives $\pi_{q+i}(T_q)\cong\pi_{q+i+1}(\Sigma T_q)$ when $q+i\le2q-2$. The unreduced suspension convention of [F5] agrees with the reduced Thom suspension after collapsing the contractible basepoint meridian; that CW collapse is a homotopy equivalence and respects the represented suspension map. For $i\le4$, $q\ge8$ satisfies both this range and step 1.2's range. Iteration identifies the actual finite-rank groups with the stable colimit. Thus [F1] gives $\pi_{q+i}(T_q)=0$ for $1\le i\le3$ and $\pi_{q+4}(T_q)=\Omega^{SO}_4$. The bottom group $\pi_q(T_q)=\mathbb Z$ is supplied by the first Hurewicz theorem and step 1.2.

The rational and odd-field calculations of [F3], with the coefficient UCT, give ranks zero for $H_2,H_3$, rank one for $H_4$, and no odd-primary torsion in these groups. Here $H_1=0$ by simple connectivity. Since $H^2(-;\mathbb F_2)$ has dimension one, $H_2$ has exactly one two-primary cyclic summand. The nonzero $Sq^1w_2$ forces this summand to have order exactly two. Explicitly, for $\mathbb Z/2^a$ the integral Bockstein of its nonzero $\mathbb F_2$-valued homomorphism is $2^{a-1}$ in $\operatorname{Ext}(\mathbb Z/2^a,\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/2^a$, whose mod-two reduction is nonzero exactly when $a=1$; a free summand has zero Bockstein. Thus $H_2=\mathbb Z/2$. The dimension-one group $H^3(-;\mathbb F_2)$ is already accounted for by $\operatorname{Ext}(H_2,\mathbb F_2)$, so $H_3/2=0$ and $H_3=0$.

Represent the integral Thom class by $f:T_q\to K(\mathbb Z,q)$. It induces an isomorphism on $\pi_q$: evaluation of the normalized class sends the bottom fiber sphere generator to one, and the first Hurewicz isomorphisms identify both groups with $\mathbb Z$. Replace $f$ by its mapping-path fibration and let $F$ be its strict fiber. Its homotopy exact sequence, the sole nonzero homotopy group of $K(\mathbb Z,q)$, and step 2.2 make $F$ $(q+3)$-connected and identify $\pi_{q+4}F$ with $\Omega^{SO}_4$. Apply the ordinary Hurewicz theorem to a CW approximation of $F$; the weak approximation induces both homotopy and integral singular-homology isomorphisms by [F6]. Consequently $\Omega^{SO}_4\cong H_{q+4}(F;\mathbb Z)$ naturally under inclusion into $T_q$.

Now $H^4(-;\mathbb F_2)$ has dimension two and $H_3=0$, so $H_4$ has exactly one two-primary cyclic summand in addition to its rank-one free part. The same cyclic-resolution calculation, applied to $Sq^1w_4=w_5\ne0$, makes that summand $\mathbb Z/2$ and makes $w_4$ evaluate nontrivially on its generator. Therefore $H_4(BSO(q);\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z/2$, and $\langle w_4,z\rangle=1$ for its nonzero torsion element $z$. This assertion is about evaluation on torsion with mod-two coefficients; it is not an integral characteristic-number evaluation.

The homological Serre sequence for $F\to T_q\to K(\mathbb Z,q)$ has only axes in total degrees through $q+5$: any mixed term needs base degree at least $q$ and fiber degree at least $q+4$. Its edge and sole possible transgression therefore give the exact segment $H_{q+5}(T_q)\to H_{q+5}(K(\mathbb Z,q))\to H_{q+4}(F)\to H_{q+4}(T_q)\xrightarrow{f_*}H_{q+4}(K(\mathbb Z,q))$. For example the middle transgression is the differential from bidegree $(q+5,0)$ to $(0,q+4)$, and all its earlier incoming/outgoing alternatives vanish by those connectivities.

The middle base group is zero by [F2]. The integral Thom isomorphism and step 4.1 therefore embed $\Omega^{SO}_4$ as $\ker f_*\subset H_{q+4}(T_q;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z/2$. Let $z'$ be its nonzero order-two element, the Thom image of $z$. By naturality and the Thom identity, $f^*(Sq^4\bar\iota_q)=Sq^4\bar u_q=w_4\bar u_q$. Evaluation on $z'$ equals one by step 4.1, so $f_*z'\ne0$. Thus the kernel contains no nonzero torsion, and $\Omega^{SO}_4$ is torsion-free. This is the integral step; a rational rank calculation alone would not prove it.

Signature is an integral homomorphism and takes the value one on $[\mathbb {CP}^2]$ by [F7]. Rational oriented bordism has rank one, so every integral class $a$ has rational image equal to $\sigma(a)[\mathbb {CP}^2]$. The difference $a-\sigma(a)[\mathbb {CP}^2]$ is therefore torsion by the rationalization criterion. It is zero by step 5.1. This proves both injectivity and surjectivity of the asserted signature map, with the stated generator.

If $\sigma(M)=0$, step 6.1 gives $[M]=0$ in the geometric oriented bordism group. By [F7] this means an actual compact oriented smooth five-manifold has oriented boundary diffeomorphic to $M$, rather than only a positive multiple of $M$. The proof never imposes a condition on $\pi_1M$. Empty inputs and finite disjoint unions are covered by the group law and the componentwise constructions in [F1]. AC is inherited exactly as in [A1].

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. The signature induces an isomorphism
$$\sigma:\Omega^{SO}_4\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathbb Z,$$
whose inverse sends $1$ to the complex-oriented projective plane. In particular every compact closed oriented smooth four-manifold $M$, with arbitrary fundamental group and any finite number of components, satisfies
$$[M]=\sigma(M)[\mathbb {CP}^{2}].$$
If $\sigma(M)=0$, then $M$ itself is the oriented boundary of a compact oriented smooth five-manifold.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

Let $(W_1,\theta_0,\theta_1)$ be a bordism from a closed smooth $n$-manifold
$M_0$ to a closed smooth $n$-manifold $M_1$, and let
$(W_2,\theta'_0,\theta'_1)$ be a bordism from $M_1$ to a closed smooth
$n$-manifold $M_2$, with the same $M_1$ in both
([[def-unoriented-smooth-cobordism-of-closed-manifolds]]). The outgoing collar
$\theta_1:(-1,0]\times M_1\to W_1$ of the first and the incoming collar
$\theta'_0:[0,1)\times M_1\to W_2$ of the second agree on $M_1\times\{0\}$ after the seam identification and
combine to a bi-collar $M_1\times(-1,1)\to W_1\cup_{M_1}W_2$; thereby they
define a smooth structure on the glued space $W=W_1\cup_{M_1}W_2$ making it a
compact smooth $(n+1)$-manifold with boundary whose seam $M_1$ is interior.
The structure is canonical for the given data: it is the maximal atlas
generated by the two given smooth structures and the bi-collar, and, assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), a change of
collar presentation changes it at most by a diffeomorphism fixed off a
neighbourhood of the seam, by the collar-comparison argument in
[[thm-the-double-has-a-well-defined-smooth-structure]]. The boundary
decomposes as $M_0\sqcup M_2$, and the outer collars $\theta_0$ and
$\theta'_1$ make $W$ a bordism from $M_0$ to $M_2$.

In the oriented theory, if both bordisms are oriented
([[def-oriented-smooth-cobordism]]), the induced orientations on the common
boundary component are opposite, the orientations glue to an orientation of
$W$, and with that orientation $W$ is an oriented bordism from $M_0$ to $M_2$.
The glued bordism and transitivity use only the supplied collars and require
no choice principle. The additional comparison of different collar systems
uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the cited comparison theorem.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

Let $M$ be a closed oriented smooth manifold of dimension $4k$, $k\ge0$, with
orientation $o$ and fundamental class
$[M]\in H_{4k}(M;\mathbb Z)$ determined by $o$
([[def-fundamental-class-of-a-compact-oriented-manifold]],
[[thm-top-homology-characterizes-compact-orientable-manifolds]]). The
**middle-dimensional intersection form** of $M$ is
$$Q_M:H^{2k}(M;\mathbb R)\times H^{2k}(M;\mathbb R)\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad Q_M(x,y):=\langle x\smile y,[M]\rangle,$$
where $\smile$ is the singular cup product of [[def-singular-cohomology-ring]]
and $\langle-,-\rangle$ is the Kronecker evaluation pairing of
[[def-kronecker-evaluation-pairing]], read on the fundamental class. The
pairing is well defined: the cup product is defined on cohomology classes and
the evaluation on classes is independent of cocycle and cycle representatives
by [[lem-the-kronecker-pairing-is-independent-of-cocycle-and-cycle-representatives]].
Since $\dim M=4k$ and both variables have degree $2k$, the product
$x\smile y$ has degree $4k$ and pairs with the top-degree class $[M]$; the
coefficient field is $\mathbb R$, with $\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb R$ as the
coefficient image.

**Integral form.** On images of integral classes the formula restricts to the
integral pairing $\langle x\smile y,[M]\rangle$ on $H^{2k}(M;\mathbb Z)$,
valued in $\mathbb Z$. The torsion subgroup of $H^{2k}(M;\mathbb Z)$ lies in
the kernel of that integral pairing; this is proved in the symmetry and
nondegeneracy lemma following on this page, not assumed here, and it is what
lets the real form be controlled by the free quotient.

**Geometric identification.** For closed oriented embedded submanifolds
$A,B\subset M$ of complementary dimension $2k$, with Poincaré duals
$\mathrm{PD}[A],\mathrm{PD}[B]\in H^{2k}(M;\mathbb Z)$ of their fundamental
classes, one has
$$Q_M(\mathrm{PD}[A],\mathrm{PD}[B])=I(A,B)=\langle A,B\rangle_M,$$
the geometric intersection number, with the cohomology-first, front-evaluation
cap and cup conventions and the geometric factor order fixed by
[[thm-geometric-intersection-equals-the-poincare-dual-cup-pairing]]; no third
sign convention is introduced
([[rem-cap-product-order-awaits-the-at-sign-convention]]).

**Disconnected and empty manifolds.** If $M=M_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup M_r$ is a
disjoint union of closed oriented components, the orientation restricts to each
component (orientability is componentwise,
[[prop-every-manifold-is-f-two-orientable-and-orientability-is-componentwise]])
and $Q_M$ is defined componentwise, on the summands of
$H^{2k}(M;\mathbb R)=\bigoplus_jH^{2k}(M_j;\mathbb R)$. For the empty manifold
one sets $Q_{\varnothing}=0$. The form is determined by this displayed formula
alone; its symmetry, nondegeneracy and additivity properties are not part of
the definition and are proved in the lemma following on this page. The pairing formula itself uses no choice principle. The geometric
identification assumes AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from its
Poincare-duality supplier.

Assume AC, inherited from the signature form and L-genus suppliers. For every
$k\ge0$, with the complex orientation of $\mathbb{CP}^{2k}$,
$$\sigma(\mathbb{CP}^{2k})=1=L[\mathbb{CP}^{2k}].$$

$\sigma(M\sqcup N)=\sigma(M)+\sigma(N)$ and $\sigma(-M)=-\sigma(M)$, where
$-M$ is $M$ with the reversed orientation. More generally $\sigma$ is additive
over disjoint unions with arbitrary orientation signs.

derivations.claim: The signed collar gluing in [F2] makes $M=(-W_0)\cup_YW_1$ a closed oriented smooth four-manifold. It uses the actual map $\phi_1^{-1}\phi_0$ on points, so no extension or mapping-class change of either boundary parametrization has been assumed. Opposite induced orientations on the two sides are exactly the compatibility condition. Fix its smooth seam collar $Y\times(-2\epsilon,2\epsilon)$.

Choose all projective-plane connected-sum balls and tubes in the interior of the nonempty $W_0$, disjoint from its boundary collar. If it has several components, any one component suffices for all insertions. The resulting $W_0'$ has exactly its previous parametrized boundary and collar. Its closed seam $M'=(-W_0')\cup_YW_1$ is the interior connected sum of $M$ with the oppositely oriented inserted projective planes. Deleting balls and applying Mayer–Vietoris, using $H_1(S^3)=H_2(S^3)=0$, identifies its second homology as the direct sum of the punctured-summand second homologies. Cycles supported in distinct summands have zero intersections. Hence the middle form is their orthogonal direct sum and $\sigma(M')=s-s=0$.

By [F1] choose an oriented smooth compact five-manifold $U$ and an orientation-preserving boundary identification $\partial U\cong M'$. Discard every component of $U$ with empty boundary. If $M'$ is connected, exactly one component remains. More generally join the finitely many remaining components by interior connected sums: remove an interior five-ball in each of two components and identify the two oriented four-sphere boundaries through $S^4\times[0,1]$ by the standard boundary-orientation-reversing gluing. Product annulus charts make this smooth and leave every original boundary collar fixed. A finite tree of these joins makes $U$ connected whenever its boundary is nonempty. Pull the seam marking and its collar back through the original boundary identification; [F2] gives an inward boundary collar of $U$. Thus near the seam there are product coordinates $Y\times(-2\epsilon,2\epsilon)_u\times[0,2\epsilon)_v$, where $v$ is inward and $u$ distinguishes the two four-dimensional pieces. This is an actual marked filling, not a claim that a boundary diffeomorphism extends across some previously chosen filling.

To identify the trace insertion explicitly, decompose $\mathbb {CP}^2$ by homogeneous coordinates $[v_0:v_1:w]$. The region $|w|^2\le c(|v_0|^2+|v_1|^2)$ is the oriented disk bundle of $\operatorname{Hom}(\gamma,\mathbb C)=\gamma^*$ over the projective line $[v_0:v_1]$, of Euler number $+1$. Its complementary region is a four-ball in the chart $w\ne0$, with coordinates $(v_0/w,v_1/w)$. The disk bundle has one zero-handle and a two-handle attached to an unknot with framing $+1$: trivialize over the two hemispheres of the base sphere; the equatorial clutching of the oriented fiber has winding one, which is exactly the attaching framing. Reverse orientation for the $-1$ version. Its boundary is the standard Hopf $S^3$, so boundary connecting this punctured projective plane to a zero/two-handle trace in a disjoint small ball is the interior connected sum. In a framed-link presentation this is adjoining a split $+1$ or $-1$ unknot, with no change to the external boundary parametrization.

The disjoint-union bordism class used by [F1] agrees with the connected-sum construction: attach a five-dimensional one-handle to $(A\sqcup B)\times[0,1]$ along one outgoing interior four-ball in each component. Its outgoing face is $A\#B$, as the two product boundary disks are replaced by the boundary cylinder of that handle. All pre-existing external boundary collars remain products. This also shows directly that no hidden cancellation or simple-connectivity theorem is being used to identify the two conventions.

Open this seam to a vertical face by removing a small notch along $Y\times\{u=v=0\}$. In the $(u,v)$ half-plane choose the remaining boundary to be a left horizontal ray, a compact smooth arc, and a right horizontal ray, unchanged outside a small rectangle. Give the arc endpoints distinct inward tangent directions from the horizontal rays, so these two points are quadrant corners. Smooth the arc only away from those endpoints and use explicit quadrant charts at the endpoints; taking its product with $Y$ defines a smooth manifold with corners. The arc becomes the vertical face $Y\times[0,1]$. The left and right boundary pieces are the original $-W_0'$ and $W_1$ with short boundary collars removed. The inward side of the chosen arc is the side retained in the region, so the orientation inherited from $U$ extends over these charts.

Identify each shortened horizontal face with its original face by a smooth increasing collar map $[0,2\epsilon)\to[\epsilon,2\epsilon)$, equal to the identity near $2\epsilon$, and the identity off that collar. Such a map is obtained by choosing a positive smooth derivative, equal to one near the far end and with the required integral on the remaining interval. Parametrize the new arc monotonically by $[0,1]$ and take the identity on $Y$; choose its endpoint parametrizations to agree with the transported horizontal collars. Thus the two corner copies of $Y$ have precisely the original maps $\phi_0,\phi_1$, point by point. The new corner charts give compatible product collars of all three faces. The induced horizontal orientations are $-W_0'$ and $W_1$; the vertical face has the boundary orientation induced from the same $U$. All notch and collar operations are confined to the chosen product neighborhood. The notch removes only a boundary collar region, and each retained point of its local half-plane model can be joined to the unchanged interior. Consequently it preserves connectedness of the chosen $U$. This constructs the stated connected $V$.

For disconnected $Y$ perform the notch construction on its finitely many disjoint collar components. If product corner strata are prescribed as part of the input, take every notch and reparametrization as the identity in those extra product coordinates; their collars remain the prescribed ones. For $Y$ empty no notch is required. None of the operations restricts or changes a fundamental-group hypothesis, and no such hypothesis was supplied. The case of two empty traces is the empty product; a lone empty $W_0$ with closed nonempty $W_1$ is outside the connected-sum clause and can instead be handled by adjoining disjoint closed projective planes. In the stated nonempty trace case all insertions and faces are exactly those constructed above.

Assume countable choice. Let $\mathcal C$ be a ribbon category with chosen left duals. Consider finite oriented framed ribbon graphs with boundary collars, bands colored by arbitrary objects of $\mathcal C$, and coupons colored by arbitrary morphisms between the tensor products of their incident signed objects. There is a unique monoidal evaluation assigning each coupon its declared morphism, crossings the braiding or its correctly typed inverse, cups/caps the chosen duality maps and their ribbon-induced opposite variants, and full twists $\theta^{\pm1}$. It is invariant under every boundary-relative framed graph isotopy and preserves composition, tensor product and the empty graph. In a strict model it is strict monoidal; transport gives the corresponding strong monoidal evaluation in $\mathcal C$.

More precisely, for a signed list $A=(Y_1^{\epsilon_1},\ldots,Y_p^{\epsilon_p})$, put $|A|=\bigotimes_sY_s^{\epsilon_s}$, with $Y^-=Y^*$. For a coupon $f:|A|\to|B|$, its strand passages and full rotation are the complete composites

$$c_{|B|,Z}(f\otimes1_Z)=(1_Z\otimes f)c_{|A|,Z},\qquad c_{Z,|B|}(1_Z\otimes f)=(f\otimes1_Z)c_{Z,|A|},\qquad\theta_{|B|}f\theta_{|A|}^{-1}=f.$$

Their tensor-list expansions, all inverse-crossing versions and the explicit dual-mate formulas supply every coupon move; the claim includes zero-input/output coupons and all band orientations. No assumption that all colors are tensor powers of one object is imposed.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a complex finite semisimple spherical ribbon category with simple unit and finite simple-label set $I$, with every $d_i\ne0$. Put $\Omega=\sum_i d_i i$ and use the multicolored arbitrary-coupon evaluator of [[lem-multicolored-ribbon-coupon-evaluation]]. The entire graph evaluation is unchanged under a framed band slide of one $\Omega$-colored surgery component over another. It is also unchanged under sliding an open strand of any fixed color, or a strand of an arbitrary coupon-bearing colored graph, over an $\Omega$-colored surgery component, keeping every original color and coupon morphism fixed. All exterior crossings, open boundary factors and coupons are included, not merely a meridian scalar or closed trace. Orientations may be reversed with dual labels; no positivity or unitarity is assumed.

Here is the exact algebraic contract. Let $B=\bigoplus_i i^*\otimes i$ with inclusions $\iota_i$. Define $\iota_X,\Delta,\varepsilon,m$ by the finite formulas in the proof, and put $\Lambda=\sum_i d_i\iota_i b_i^R$. Then

$$m(1_B\otimes\Lambda)=\Lambda\varepsilon,\qquad\Gamma=(1_B\otimes m)(\Delta\otimes1_B),\qquad\Gamma(1_B\otimes\Lambda)=1_B\otimes\Lambda,\qquad\Gamma(\Lambda\otimes\Lambda)=\Lambda\otimes\Lambda.$$

For a fixed object $Y$ the lifted open-strand operator, retaining its entire first tensor factor, is

$$\widehat\Gamma_Y=(1_{Y^*\otimes Y}\otimes m)(1_{Y^*\otimes Y}\otimes\iota_Y\otimes1_B)(1_{Y^*}\otimes b_Y\otimes1_Y\otimes1_B),$$

and it satisfies $\widehat\Gamma_Y(1_{Y^*\otimes Y}\otimes\Lambda)=1_{Y^*\otimes Y}\otimes\Lambda$. Its exterior requires dinaturality only in the surgery-component variable; there is no naturality assumption on an arbitrary family of graph coupons indexed by $Y$. This lemma has no Gauss-sum, Fenn–Rourke, surgery normalization or topological move-completeness premise.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a complex modular spherical ribbon fusion category. Put $D^2=\sum_i d_i^2$, choose $D\ne0$, let $p_\pm=\sum_i\theta_i^{\pm1}d_i^2$, $\kappa=p_+/D$, and $\Omega=\sum_i d_i i$. Write $b_X:\mathbf1\to X\otimes X^*$ and $e_X:X^*\otimes X\to\mathbf1$ for left duality, $r_X=e_{X^*}(j_X\otimes1)$ for right evaluation, and $b_X^R=(1\otimes j_X^{-1})b_{X^*}$ for right coevaluation. For $a:X\otimes Z\to Y\otimes Z$ define

$$\operatorname{ptr}_Z(a)=(1_Y\otimes r_Z)(a\otimes1_{Z^*})(1_X\otimes b_Z),\qquad M_{X,Z}=c_{Z,X}c_{X,Z}.$$

Then $p_+p_-=D^2$, and the following are identities of complete morphisms, valid with arbitrary exterior tensor factors and coupons:

$$K_\pm(X):=\sum_i d_i\theta_i^{\pm1}\operatorname{ptr}_i(M_{X,i}^{\pm1})=p_\pm\theta_X^{\mp1}.$$

The zero-framed meridian operator $E_X=\sum_i d_i\operatorname{ptr}_i(M_{X,i})$ equals $D^2P_X$, where $P_X$ is the projection onto the full unit-isotypic summand. For $a\in\operatorname{End}(i^*\otimes j)$ define

$$R_{ij}(a)=(r_i\otimes1_j\otimes1_{j^*})(1_i\otimes a\otimes1_{j^*})(1_i\otimes1_{i^*}\otimes b_j).$$

The paired-handle/coupon contraction is

$$R_{ij}(E_{i^*\otimes j})=\delta_{ij}\frac{D^2}{d_i}1_{i\otimes i^*}.$$

Thus the normalized graph evaluation $D^{-m-1}\kappa^{-\sigma(B)}F$ is unchanged under a signed generalized Fenn–Rourke twist-surgery move or circumcision adding a framed knot and its small zero-framed meridian. These are local algebraic identities; a complete presentation/move theorem is a separate topological assertion. No positivity, unitary conjugation, or anomaly cancellation is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For each filling torus choose oriented coordinates $V_i=D^2_z\times S^1_\theta$, with dual core $c_i=\{0\}\times S^1$ and filling meridian $\mu_i=\partial D^2\times\{\theta_0\}$. Its boundary gluing sends $\mu_i$ to the specified framed parallel $\lambda_i$, with the sign induced by the fixed orientation convention. Extend its radial coordinate across the boundary into a disjoint exterior collar, so $0\le r\le1+\epsilon$, $V_i=\{r\le1\}$. Those neighborhoods are disjoint from $C$. A finite ribbon graph has a finite fatgraph spine: each coupon retracts to its labeled vertex with ordered short incident arcs, each band to its core edge, and a coupon-free annulus to a circle edge. Shrinking coupon rectangles and band widths gives a genuine ambient isotopy to any sufficiently narrow thickening of that spine, not a collapse to zero width. In a band chart this is a smooth coordinate contraction of its width variable, extended by a cutoff to a surrounding box; in a coupon chart contract its disk and join the moved bases by short parallel strips, keeping their order. These finitely many charts glue on their product collars; on $C$ no width or base is changed. The ribbon's orientation and transverse width vector keep its full framing during this isotopy.

Perturb the compact interior spine slightly so all its vertices and edges avoid every $c_i$. A vertex is zero-dimensional and a core one-dimensional in dimension three, and an edge has dimension one, so their incidence has negative expected dimension. This can be obtained by [F4] with chart cutoffs away from the endpoint/coupon collars. Perturbations sufficiently small preserve the finite embedded graph, attachment order and framing; then narrow its thickening so it also misses the cores. If its smallest radial coordinate in a torus is $\delta>0$, choose a smooth increasing function $\phi:[0,1+\epsilon]\to[0,1+\epsilon]$ that is linear near0, the identity near $1+\epsilon$, and has $\phi(\delta)>1+\epsilon/2$. Such a function is obtained by integrating a positive smooth derivative with most of its mass before $\delta$, then normalizing its total integral; the derivative can be constant near0 and1 near the outer endpoint. The interpolation $\phi_s=(1-s)r+s\phi(r)$ has positive derivative. The maps $(z,\theta)\mapsto(\phi_s(|z|)z/|z|,\theta)$ are therefore smooth ambient isotopies, including at the core by the linear behavior. They fix the outside of the extended torus and push every graph point in it to $r>1$. Applying these finitely many disjoint radial isotopies puts the whole graph in the exterior, proving part (1).

Now take a framed graph isotopy in the filled manifold between two exterior representatives. Work on the transported abstract spine, retaining its ordered labeled vertices and all fixed collar endpoints. On each edge, its track is a smooth map from an interval times the isotopy interval to $Y_L$; the inverse image of the codimension-two core set has dimension zero after a small relative perturbation. Vertex tracks have dimension one and can avoid the cores entirely. For precision, take finitely many normal-coordinate charts near the cores and finite source charts on the compact edge tracks, with cutoff perturbations of their two normal coordinates. At each proposed incidence these parameters span the normal directions; [F4] makes the tracks transverse. Independent perturbations at two distinct edge parameters exclude simultaneous double incidences: two core conditions impose four equations on the two edge parameters and their common time, a three-dimensional domain. A further jet condition excludes a nontransverse individual incidence. No incidence is allowed at the fixed time endpoints, graph vertices or boundary collars, all of which already have disjoint neighborhoods. The small perturbation remains a family of spatial embeddings: derivatives on each edge remain nonzero, and compact sets of separated source pairs remain separated; the fixed local vertex charts preserve attachment order. Frame vectors extend by the same nearby normal charts. Thus it is an isotopy, not a generic homotopy allowing graph crossings.

The core incidences are a closed zero-dimensional transverse subset of finitely many compact track strips, with none near their boundaries or vertices, hence finite. Separate their times. Between small disjoint event intervals the spine stays a positive distance from the cores, so choose the radial expansion of step 2.1 uniformly on each closed time interval and then a sufficiently narrow ribbon thickening. This gives a genuine exterior graph isotopy on that interval. Different expansions at an interval endpoint give exterior-isotopic graphs: interpolate their positive radial functions after first choosing a common lower clearance; their convex interpolation still puts every point at $r>1$. The initial and terminal representatives can be kept exactly as given by choosing the outer radial collars disjoint from their compact graphs and taking the time cutoff to vanish there. Therefore it remains only to compute the local change at each of the finitely many spine/core events.

At one event write the original time offset as $\tau_0=t-t_0$. Transversality says the derivative of its two normal coordinates with respect to $(u_0,\tau_0)$ is invertible. Rotate the target normal plane so the edge derivative is $(a,0)$, $a>0$, and write the time derivative $(b,c)$ with $c\ne0$. Make only the fiber-preserving linear changes $u=a u_0+b\tau_0$ and $\tau=c\tau_0$. Thus each new time slice is one original time slice, possibly with a constant reversal of its order, and the normal map is $z=(u,\tau)+R(u,\tau)$ with $R=O((|u|+|\tau|)^2)$ and $DR=O(|u|+|\tau|)$. In a sufficiently small source disk choose a cutoff $\chi$ equal to1 on its central half and zero near its boundary, and interpolate to $z_s=(u,\tau)+(1-s\chi)R$ while leaving the original time parameter fixed. On a disk of radius $\rho$, $|z_s|\ge r-Cr^2\ge r/2$ for $r=\sqrt{u^2+\tau^2}>0$ after choosing $\rho$ small; its derivative is $I+O(\rho)$, including the cutoff derivative because $D\chi=O(\rho^{-1})$ and $R=O(\rho^2)$. Hence no extra core zero or degenerate zero is introduced, and every fixed-time arc remains embedded. The perturbation is supported away from the local arc's endpoints, all other graph pieces and coupon/boundary collars; its smallness preserves the spatial embedding family and framing. The resulting normal map is exactly $z=u+i\tau$ on the central event region, with unchanged nonzero connecting arcs outside it. Its longitudinal coordinate is a smooth function of those normal coordinates; subtract that function in a static small target core chart to obtain $\theta=\theta_0$. This target coordinate change mixes no source time with the edge parameter. Thus the before/after local arcs are the upper/lower detours $z=u\pm i\eta$ in the punctured meridional disk. Multiply the displacement by a source cutoff equal to1 near the event and zero near the ends of the local arc; equivalently round the two short end connectors in the core-free outer collar. This makes their endpoints exactly the same, joined to the identical unchanged exterior arcs. After radial expansion, the two detours differ by one circuit of $\partial D^2\times\{\theta_0\}$, with sign determined by the transverse incidence. To verify this without a drawing, choose a continuous argument on each detour: its change from negative to positive $u$ is approximately $-\pi$ on the upper arc and $+\pi$ on the lower, so the difference of the two relative homotopy classes is one signed $2\pi$ meridian. The region between either detour and the corresponding boundary arcs is an embedded disk after a small collar rounding, giving an actual relative arc isotopy, not only a homotopy classification. Gluing by the given torus map converts that based meridian circuit to a band sum with $\pm\lambda_i$, precisely the framed open-strand slide over the original surgery component.

This local calculation lifts to the whole framed ribbon. Choose a trivialization of its oriented normal plane over the event track disk, which is contractible; the original framing is an actual nonzero vector field there and extends in that trivialization. Take the small product strip thickening of the before/after detours and of the connecting meridional disk. The filling boundary gluing carries that strip along the specified surgery framing on $\lambda_i$. Radial expansion transports the same vectors by its differential. Hence the resulting band slide has exactly the transported normal framing; no Reidemeister-I curl is dropped. Any preexisting rotation of the strip is retained on both sides. Both signed incidences and both strand orientations are handled directly; if one chooses instead to reverse a label its dual and its actual bend maps are used, rather than identifying the two oriented band moves without their twists. Coupon neighborhoods have core-free vertex tracks, so the finite event balls can be chosen disjoint from all coupons and boundary collars. After each event choose a positive small width for the actual ribbons at its two exterior slices; a zero-width ribbon at the event time is neither required nor used. Outside the event ball the original product strips and coupons are unchanged. Combining all finite events and regular intervals proves part (2).

Every colored operation in part (2) keeps the original coupon morphisms as actual fixed maps. For a simple local strand $j$, its band slide is [F2]'s identity on the full $j^*\otimes j$ factor after bending, with its fixed exterior pre/post-composed. For a general color $X$, insert the actual finite resolution $1_X=\sum_{j,a}u_{j,a}v^{j,a}$ on a short segment disjoint from coupons; absorb those two actual morphisms into the adjacent fixed exterior portions, apply the fixed-$j$ identity, then sum. The inverse dual-mate snakes unbend the equality to the original open graph morphism before closure. Only the surgery-component variable is dinatural; no arbitrary family of graph coupons depending on variable $X$ is introduced. Exterior colored isotopies preserve evaluation by [F1]. Thus the extra moves used to compare two exterior representatives have the full arbitrary-coupon algebraic invariance required in the Statement.

We next show that the canonical undecorated local moves admit the needed graph lifts. For an $O2$ band slide, put the graph spine transverse to the attaching rectangle and move its finitely many coupon vertices off it. There are finitely many interior intersections, since its short attaching edges lie on the surgery tori and the exterior graph misses those tori. Each of the rectangle's two long edges is free: it is not part of the surgery link. For one graph intersection choose a simple path in the rectangle to the interior of a free long edge, avoiding the other intersection points and both attaching edges. A thin strip about this path is a disk whose neighborhood is a ball disjoint from the surgery link, all coupon vertices, and all graph portions except the intersecting short arc. Push that arc's transverse crossing along the strip and around the free edge. In disk-product coordinates the move replaces a short normal interval through the strip by a U-shaped detour outside its boundary; the swept disk has interior disjoint from the rest of the graph and the link. The cutoff flow in this ball realizes an actual framed graph isotopy, with the normal framing transported. The new arc misses the rectangle, and the strip's choice prevents new intersections. Repeat finitely many times. This preparation is entirely an exterior graph isotopy; no unjustified naturality or disk bounding an arbitrary longitude is needed. After narrowing the ribbons, the actual graph misses a neighborhood of the band and both surgery tori. The standard canonical $O2$ filling identification is the identity outside that neighborhood, so the undecorated surgery-component slide now carries this graph unchanged in exterior coordinates. Both directions use the same construction with their respective rectangles.

For an $O1$ insertion, its ball and a slightly larger ball miss the old surgery link. The graph can be moved out of the support ball by an exterior ambient isotopy: choose a point there off its thin spine, shrink the support ball into a tiny ball about that point using a smooth radial contraction extended to the slightly larger ball, and apply the inverse contraction to the graph. The tiny ball is disjoint from the graph, so its inverse image is disjoint from the original support ball. This fixes collars and the old link. Now introduce the separated $\pm1$ unknot with graph unchanged; the canonical filling map fixes its exterior. For deletion, use the canonical filled-ball identification to perform this graph-avoidance isotopy in that ball first, then translate it to the current surgery exterior by parts (1)–(2). The graph is then disjoint from the deletion support. If one uses the equivalent local signed twist-surgery description with strands passing through its disk, its complete colored lift is also [F3]'s arbitrary-coupon identity; no additional graph move is required.

For an $O3$ insertion, perturb its introduced framed knot $K$ slightly off the finite graph spine, keeping it disjoint from the old surgery link and all boundary collars. This is an isotopy of the prescribed local move data, with its framing transported, so its canonical marked identification changes only by the corresponding rel-collar isotopy. Narrow the graph and choose the support tube $N(K)$ disjoint from it, then introduce its small zero-framed meridian there. The canonical circumcision filling identification is the identity outside that tube, so the graph is unchanged. For deletion, carry the current graph to the output of that canonical identification. A spine can first be made disjoint from $K$ and then pushed outside $N(K)$ by the explicit core-avoidance/radial construction of step 1.1, step 2.1, now applied to that ordinary tube. Pull that isotopy back through the specified identification and translate it to the current surgery exterior by parts (1)–(2). The deletion support is then graph-free. Its evaluation invariance is [F3]'s complete circumcision identity, with the preliminary graph changes covered by [F2]. No nullhomotopy of $K$ or assumption that the ambient manifold is simply connected is used.

Invoke the marked undecorated hypothesis only now. Given a marked bordism, take its supplied undecorated surgery presentation and pull the actual decoration back along its specified output identification. step 2.1 puts it in the exterior, preserving every terminal parametrization/collar ribbon. Given two marked decorated presentations of the same decoration, take the supplied finite undecorated sequence realizing their specified output identification up to rel-collar isotopy. Lift each exterior link isotopy by its ambient isotopy and each $O1/O2/O3$ by step 6.2, step 7.1, step 7.2, inserting their finite preparatory graph moves as necessary. Every lifted step represents the graph transported by that very canonical move map, up to a rel-collar graph isotopy. This is why the marked realization hypothesis, not bare existence of an unspecified diffeomorphism, is the exact global input needed here.

After that finite lifted sequence, the graph in the last exterior is isotopic in the filled output to the prescribed final graph: their output markings agree up to the given rel-collar isotopy, and they represent the same marked decoration. Part (2) converts precisely this last graph isotopy into the allowed finite exterior isotopies and open-strand slides. All coupon labels, endpoint intervals, attachment orders, band orientations and framings were carried throughout; no new boundary intersection was introduced because every perturbation/expansion was supported outside $C$. The argument is componentwise over finitely many manifold components and allows closed graph components, zero-valence coupons and empty boundary components. The total extra graph-move sequence preserves evaluation by step 6.1, and the local link-move algebra is [F2]–[F3]. This proves the full stated decorated lifting implication, conditional only on the actual marked undecorated calculus in part (3), without claiming that global calculus or any colored Cerf theorem has thereby been proved.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume full AC. Let $W$ be a compact smooth $n$-manifold, $n\ge1$, with fixed product collars, and let $f_0,f_1:W\to[0,1]$ be excellent adapted Morse functions equal to the same noncritical product height on those collars. There is a smooth path $F_s$ joining them, stationary near its parameter endpoints and fixed on smaller boundary collars, with finitely many exceptional parameters. Each exceptional parameter contains exactly one of: a corank-one interior birth/death with nonzero kernel cubic and nonzero parameter unfolding, or a transverse crossing of two nondegenerate critical values. All other critical points are nondegenerate, all other critical values are distinct, no two events share a parameter, and a birth value differs from every other critical value. The critical locus is a compact smooth curve whose parameter projection has only nondegenerate folds. Each fold creates or destroys two critical points of adjacent indices with distinct critical values. By a homotopy supported near each fold, preserving this event list and the endpoints, the path can further be put near that fold in smooth parameter-dependent spatial coordinates into the form

$$F_s=a(s)+b(s)u+c_0u^3+Q(y),\qquad b(0)=0,\quad b'(0)\ne0,\quad c_0>0,$$

where $Q$ is a fixed nondegenerate quadratic form in $n-1$ variables. Empty ends, disconnected $W$, and index $0/n$ pairs are allowed. This is a function-path statement with fixed product height; it has no boundary critical events and asserts no global descending-field or surgery-move theorem.

Assume full AC. On a compact smooth collared bordism, keep the incoming and outgoing parametrizations as part of a finite elementary handle description. A generic adapted function path supplied by [[lem-relative-one-parameter-morse-path-with-finite-events]] induces a finite sequence of changes of its Morse-induced elementary handle descriptions: relative diffeomorphisms and isotopies of the framed attaching embeddings, changes of standard handle-coordinate frame, splitting/merging empty product bands, interchange of two independent disjoint framed attachments, and creation/removal of a geometrically cancelling adjacent-index pair. At every change retain the induced outgoing boundary map and carry every later attaching embedding and final boundary parametrization by it. Changes of descending field within a single elementary band alter its framed attaching embedding and outgoing map only by the corresponding isotopies. The birth cancellation has exactly one connecting trajectory. Disconnected bordisms, empty ends, and index $0/n$ pairs are included.

This is a comparison of parametrized elementary bands with their actual cancellation boundary maps retained. It does not suppress those maps, classify an arbitrary global path of descending fields by slides, or assert surgery/Kirby/coupon completeness.

Let $m\ge 0$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^m$ be open around
$(0,0)$, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth with

$$F(0,0)=0,\qquad \frac{\partial F}{\partial u}(0,0)=0,\qquad \frac{\partial^2F}{\partial u^2}(0,0)\ne0.$$

Then, after shrinking $U$, there are a sign $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$, a smooth
function $H$ of the parameter variable, and a smooth local coordinate
change $(u,y)\mapsto (u',y)$ fixing $(0,0)$ such that

$$F(u,y)=H(y)+\varepsilon (u')^2.$$

Let $k,m,n\ge1$ and $p\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n+p}$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^k$. Suppose $F(a,b,\lambda_0)=0$ and $D_yF(a,b,\lambda_0)$ is invertible. Then there are neighbourhoods and a unique $C^k$ map $\varphi$ solving $F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)=0$. More precisely, on suitable open neighbourhoods $P$ of $(a,\lambda_0)$ and $Q$ of $b$,

$$F(x,y,\lambda)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x,\lambda),$$

and

$$D\varphi(x,\lambda)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)^{-1}D_{(x,\lambda)}F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda).$$

When no parameter block is present, this is the ordinary $C^k$ implicit function theorem.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. For each $p\in M$, let
$\gamma_p:I_p\to M$ be the maximal integral curve through $p$, and set

$$ \mathcal D:=\{(t,p)\in\mathbb R\times M:t\in I_p\}, \qquad \Phi(t,p):=\gamma_p(t). $$

Then $\mathcal D$ is open in $\mathbb R\times M$, each fibre $\mathcal D_p$ is
an interval containing $0$, the map $\Phi:\mathcal D\to M$ is smooth, and
$\Phi$ is the unique maximal local flow generated by $X$.

Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a compact interval, and let $X_t$ be a smooth
time-dependent vector field on $M$ such that

$$ \bigcup_{t\in J}\operatorname{supp}(X_t) $$

is contained in a compact subset $K\subseteq M$. Then there is a global evolution
operator $\Psi_{t,s}:M\to M$ for all $s,t\in J$.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold with boundary admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $K\subseteq M$ be compact, and let $W\subseteq M$ be open with $K\subseteq W$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:M\to [0,1]$ that equals $1$ on an open neighbourhood of $K$ and satisfies $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq W$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every subset of a manifold null set is
null, and every countable union of manifold null sets is null.

Let $M$ be a positive-dimensional smooth manifold, let $\mathcal A$ be a smooth
atlas on $M$, and let $E\subseteq M$ be $\mathcal A$-null in the sense of
[[def-null-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold]]. Then $M\setminus E$ is dense in $M$.
In particular, under Countable Choice the conclusion holds for any manifold-null
set $E$.
Under countable choice, every smooth manifold, also with boundary, admits a Riemannian metric.

On a connected Riemannian manifold define $d_g(p,q)=\inf\{L_g(\gamma):\gamma\text{ is piecewise }C^1\text{ from }p\text{ to }q\}$.

Lengths are those of [[def-riemannian-speed-and-length]]. For each pair $p,q$, [[lem-any-two-points-in-a-connected-smooth-manifold-can-be-joined-by-a-piecewise-c-one-curve]] supplies a curve, so the set of lengths is nonempty, contains a finite real number and is bounded below by zero. Applying the least-upper-bound property [[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]] to the negatives gives a finite nonnegative infimum. On the empty connected manifold this defines the empty distance function; there are no pairs to evaluate. No minimizing curve is part of this definition.
$d_g$ is a finite metric on a connected Riemannian manifold.
The topology of $d_g$ is the manifold topology on every connected Riemannian manifold.

For a compact set $K$ contained in one coordinate chart of an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold, there are $0<c\le C<\infty$ such that $c|v|^2\le g_x(v,v)\le C|v|^2$ for $x\in K$. The dimension-zero assertion is vacuous.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be any topological space, let $Y$ be a compact metric space, and let $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Y)$ be equicontinuous. Then the compact-open closure of $\mathcal F$ is compact.
Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $Y$ be a metric space. On $C(X,Y)$, the published compact-open topology is equal to the topology of uniform convergence.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and the Axiom
of Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]).** Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]). Then the following five conditions are equivalent.

- **(a)** $(X,d)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
- **(b)** $(X,d)$ is countably compact ([[def-metric-compactness-variants]]).
- **(c)** $(X,d)$ is limit point compact.
- **(d)** $(X,d)$ is sequentially compact.
- **(e)** $(X,d)$ is complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]) and totally bounded
  ([[def-totally-bounded]]).

**The two hypotheses are not needed everywhere, and the statement should not be
read as if they were.** Of the implications assembled below, all but two are
theorems of ZF. Dependent choice is used only for "sequentially compact implies
totally bounded" ([[thm-sequentially-compact-implies-totally-bounded]]), and
countable choice only for "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]). Each is an upper bound on
the cost of the proof given in this library and not a claim of necessity; the
implication-by-implication account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].
